subsubtopic: LEGISLATION REQUIRING CORPORATIONS TO DISCLOSE EXECUTIVE SALARIES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that the federal government's Anti-Inflation Board held back wage increases for working Canadians, in view of the revelation by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission that a top Hudson Bay Oil Company executive had his wages increased by $38,000 last year, from $141,000 to $ 179,000, up 27 per cent, that a Hiram Walker executive had his wages increased by $23,000 last year, up 22 per cent, and in view of the fact that these companies are not required to disclose this information under Canadian law, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That this House calls upon the government to require the Anti-Inflation Board to roll back these wage increases to the supposed $2,400 annual maximum, and that this House urge the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to bring forward legislation requiring corporations doing business in Canada to disclose their executive salaries.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgency pertaining to the recent discovery and use by the Soviet Union of a tunnel and of electronic eavesdropping devices at the United States embassy in Moscow. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle):
That the House deplores and condemns such actions by the Soviet Union which are not at all in keeping with the spirit of detente which that country advocates between the east and west; further, that the House calls upon the Soviet Union to desist from such practices against the United States or against any other country and supports any protest on the matter made to the Soviet Union by the United States; and, finally, the House strongly suggests that the Secretary of State for External Affairs take whatever steps may be necessary to guarantee that no similar situation exists at the Canadian embassy in Moscow, if indeed such steps have not been taken already.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN GRAIN SHIPMENTS THROUGH CHURCHILL, MAN -MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent priority. No serious effort is being shown by this government to increase grain shipments through the port of Churchill this season. The reduced rail distance from Yorkton to Churchill, as opposed to Yorkton to Vancouver and Prince Rupert, would guarantee a quicker turnaround time on boxcars, Yorkton to Vancouver being 1,301 miles, Yorkton to Prince Rupert 1,493 miles, and Yorkton to Churchill 722 miles. Therefore, bearing in mind that the port of Churchill is underutilized and that this port is the most efficient grain handling port in Canada, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta):
That the government direct the Wheat Board to increase grain shipments by a minimum of five million bushels this season through the port of Churchill to help relieve the intolerable tie-up at Vancouver.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact the federal government has refused to return the oil tax money to Indian bands in Alberta and Saskatchewan which totals approximately $4.5 million, in view of the fact the government's refusal to return these funds has prevented the Indian communities from developing the necessary infrastructure which is desperately needed to correct long-standing social economic problems, and in view of the fact the government policy increases the Indians' dependence on the public purse and a paternalistic government, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith):
That the government immediately act on the suggestion of my colleague from Wetaskiwin and establish a tripartite meeting to resolve this important problem.

speechtext:
I have a question for the same minister, Mr. Speaker. I would point out to him that, as he well knows, housing and urban affairs are within the jurisdiction of the provinces, not the federal government. It is clearly an intrusion into provincial rights for this government to initiate housing.
In view of the fact that the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, one of our major mortgage lenders, has indicated that it will not participate in the new guaranteed payment mortgage program of the government, and that the Royal Bank has said it will participate only to a limited degree, would the hon. gentleman tell the House why he proceeded with the program without first obtaining an agreement or assurance from the major mortgage lenders in this country that the program was satisfactory? Indeed, Mr. Speaker, since the Canadian Bankers' Association told the minister in February that the program was unacceptable, why did the hon. gentleman proceed with such a project?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR RENEGOTIATION OF NEW POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know where the hon. member finds his foundation for the statement that housing is a matter of provincial jurisdiction. The federal government clearly has a national mandate to ensure that all people living in Canada, whether in one part or another, have a right to decent housing. Throughout the years the Canadian government has been fulfilling its obligation in this respect and will continue to do so despite what the hon. member says or what may be the view of the Conservative party.

In relation to the graduated payment mortgage, I wish to tell the hon. member that we do not ask that all lenders make such loans. We know that some lenders will participate and we expect that other lenders will not. I am not surprised by the conservative approach to the program taken by some of the banks, but I believe credit unions and caisses populates will support the program-one which has proved very popular and which has been actively supported in the United States. We believe it could be beneficial to many young families in Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and it concerns the fisheries dispute. Reports suggest that the next meeting of the negotiators on the fisheries boundaries delineation agreement will not be until June 19. In light of what happened over the weekend, can the minister say whether he has decided to have that meeting updated and called earlier; and if not, why not? Why is it necessary to wait for a fortnight, for example? Does he expect that the U.S. Congress might be forced, as a result of this delay, to ratify the agreement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: RATIFICATION OF FISHERIES AGREEMENT WITH U.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of elements in the question. Of course, there is nothing to prevent the Congress from proceeding, nor have we heard anything to the contrary, with ratification of the agreement. I said on Friday, in answer to questions here, that it is more the interpretation of the agreement than a willingness to actually endorse it that is at the root of the present problem. Therefore, it could proceed. Whether or not it will, I cannot anticipate.
On the second question of the time delay between the decision to act as we did on Friday and the first meeting, this was discussed prior to the actual introduction of the measures and the conclusion was that this was, first of all, I think, the

earliest practical date on which the two negotiators could get together. I might suggest, without going too deeply into it, that it may be useful to let a little time go by before the negotiators get back to the table, so as to perhaps get some evidence of what the public reaction is going to be.

subsubtopic: RATIFICATION OF FISHERIES AGREEMENT WITH U.S.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is related to the ratification procedure in the U.S. If, for example-this might sound hypothetical-the Congress were to ratify the agreement, would the agreement be in effect and would we be going back to the discussions on the long-term agreement; or is it a matter of implementation? I think the House and the country should have clarification on that point.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: RATIFICATION OF FISHERIES AGREEMENT WITH U.S.
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. It is not at all hypothetical. There is, I repeat, some possibility that the U.S. Congress might wish to do so, if for no other reason than, for example, there were to be a permanent agreement put into place. As I understand it, there would be an interregnum period during which there would be no mechanism through which the U.S. authorities could act. It is complicated, and I would be glad to have a written answer given to the hon. member's question. If the written agreement were to be ratified by the United States, it would not be our intention, nor that of the United States, I suspect, to go back to negotiating the interpretation of that agreement for the next few months.
It is possible that something might be developed rather quickly, but it is the joint view of both countries that the negotiators should now proceed directly to negotiation of a long-term agreement and they will be concentrating their efforts on that. But if the agreement were in place in the U.S. and if there was a disposition, as a result of the actions of the past weekend, to put an end more formally to any tensions, then of course the means would be there by which it could be done.

Le depute Baldwin n'a pas a s'eriger en Cour d'appel pour etudier la conduite du juge presidant le proces, d'autant plus qu'il esl dans la plus complete

I have the conviction, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Peace River, with all his experience as a lawyer and parliamentarian, could not have made those statements had he known that Mr. Treu's lawyer had agreed to both the preliminary hearing and the trial being held in camera, which can be deduced from the statement issued by Judge Mayrand, and I cannot blame the hon. member for Peace River for not having understood it, since the translation of that part of Judge Mayrand is very poor.

That being the fact, one must also ask oneself, Mr. Speaker, if the principles contained in the judge's statement lend themselves to a question of privilege. Now, there are two of these principles which are unequivocal and which, I believe, contain nothing irregular or reprehensible. The first principle set out by the judge is as follows, and I quote:

The second and last principle set out by the judge in his statement is as follows, and I quote:
In any circumstances, public interest and the preservation of individual liberties demand that we strictly adhere to the principle of separation of the three powers, that is the executive, the legislative and the judiciary; each citizen must respect their rights and privileges and especially those who hold a position with great responsibilities as is the case for a Member of Parliament.

To attempt to influence members in their conduct by threats is also a breach of privilege.
Mr. Speaker, there is absolutely nothing in Judge May-rand's comments that is a real threat to the hon. member's privileges or rights. There is no threat of steps to be taken against the hon. member, there is no threat that the judge adopt any behaviour or take any measure to limit the privileges or the rights of the hon. member or of members of this House.
So this fine principle of Erskine May could not be applied here because the facts do not justify it. Nor do the other two fine principles of Erskine May at pages 151 and 153, as referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The second principle was, and I quote:
It is a breach of privilege to molest any member of either House on account of his conduct in Parliament.
What molestation is there in this statement by Judge Mayrand? Obviously, Mr. Speaker, there is absolutely no molestation involved.
And the third principle raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, still based on Erskine May, was, and I quote:
Wilful misrepresentation of the proceedings of members is an offence of the same character as a libel.
Here again, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the facts contained in this statement as well as the principles and their form do not constitute in any way a wilful misrepresentation of the proceedings of members of this House.
These worthy principles which do not have any reference to the facts contained in the statement of Judge Mayrand cannot be applied here and give ground to the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Peace River. On the contrary, the only passages which might be interpreted as indicating to that member a line of conduct, these only passages, I repeat,
Privilege-Mr. Baldwin
are literally reverential. You just have to take a look at what is suggested by the judge: First he says
We respectfully advise him to content himself with doing his own work,-
And the second passage where the judge might be interpreted as giving a piece of advice to the hon. member is, and I quote:
It seems to us that it would be preferable to leave to the courts the delicate task of drawing the line between the rights of the individual and the rights of a nation in the application of the law.
So when the hon. member is respectfully being advised about something and when the judge says:
It seems to us that it would be preferable ...
I respectfully submit this was suggested in a reverent fashion, to say the least, and there is nothing in the nature of a threat to the hon. member, neither in the comments nor in the form of the statement by Judge Mayrand.
Mr. Speaker, I would note further that this is neither a judgment nor an order, but a mere comment, a mere criticism. Since there is nothing in the statement made by the sessions court deputy chief judge, either in fact, in principle or in form, that might be considered even a beginning of an infringement on our privileges, it would be surprising if the title or function of the originator justified the proposal made by the hon. member for Peace River. Whether he is a judge or a private citizen, because this has been raised, is not relevant in the circumstances. And therefore the distinction made by certain speakers, including the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, for the reason that a judge may or might hold the hon. member for Peace River for contempt is groundless. The hon. member for Peace River has enjoyed and still enjoys parliamentary immunity. Therefore, the danger that some high-tempered member of parliament be held in contempt by a judge he criticized is no greater than that of his being sprayed with water by some fireman he might criticize. Whether it be a judge or a fireman, or anyone for that matter that the hon. member may criticize under his parliamentary immunity, there is absolutely no danger for the member.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, the judge's statement is neither a judgment nor an order, but a mere comment included in a release. It is not even an obiter dictum in the body of a judicial decision. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, may I refer to a decision made by yourself on December 5, 1977, in the matter of a judgment by Mr. Justice Evans, Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Ontario, on the motion by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That the portions of the judgment of Chief Justice Evans of the Supreme Court of Ontario, given November 9, 1977, which appear to restrict the right of members of parliament to full and accurate reporting in the press, be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
Mr. Speaker, you stated in your ruling, and I quote very briefly from that decision on page 1541 of Hansard for December 5, 1977:

June 5, 1978
Privilege-Mr. Baldwin
I understand the reasoning of the Chief Justice in having to do so, and in the generalized way in which he dealt with matters outside Parliament. In my opinion, he created no addition to the law which in any way lessens the privileges of members of this House.
Finally, even if he had done so, his pronouncement is obiter dicta clearly, by any understanding of any lawyer who examines his reasoning and is entirely theoretical in nature.
Mr. Speaker, may I remind the House of the merits of your own remarks which were made before the House last Thursday, as shown at page 5953 of Hansard, and I understand that it was not a formal decision, but I want to conclude with the following remarks, Mr. Speaker, and I quote:
Of course my obligation may be to find whether the matter does in fact come within the strict and classic definition of privilege that we have followed in the past, whether there has been an affront or contempt of parliament, or whether there has been a molestation or interference in some way with the hon. member in carrying out his duty.
And you added further, and I quote:
... and since language has often been set aside as an actual molestation and interference, and since obviously the hon. member and other hon. members are not in the slightest intimidated in their desire to pursue this matter, by whatever language was used ...
... but it may be difficult to fit them into the specific and classic definition of privilege...
Finally, I would to remind the limit of our privileges as it is very clearly prescribed in the fourth edition of Beauchesne's Parliament Rules and Forms, page 94, and I quote:
... the only privilege remaining to members beyond the walls of St. Stephen's were freedom from arrest, assault, insult or menace in their coming and going from the House, and inviolability, so far as the outside world was concerned, for their utterances within the Chamber; and these are the only privileges enjoyed to-day by the Canadian Parliament under section 18 of the B.N.A Act...
Therefore, if under the cover of parliamentary immunity a member of parliament can say anything or almost anything without running the risk of being sued, we cannot extend the present scope of our privileges to the censorship of what has been said by people from outside who comment honestly on the use which has been made of these privileges. As to knowing, Mr. Speaker, whether the statement issued by Judge Mayrand was timely or not, and whether judges should make declarations at all on highly political questions, to debate this matter here would not help whatsoever in solving the question of determining the privileges of hon. members.

Mr. Speaker, I have tried to make this motion an all-encompassing one. Your Honour probably realized that when reading it. I will not belabour the House with that again. However, I want to deal with the motion section by section. I want to begin by saying, for the benefit of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), who is in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, that all sides of this House have always approved of the acquisition of hopper cars. It has received the support not just of members of parliament but also of grain organizations, grain producers and, I think, the public generally.
We recognize and applaud the amount of grain that is being moved, and that we may obtain a record grain movement, or close to it, this year. We say thank you. We will even give some credit to the minister. I hope he will not use up any time in his speech repeating what he has been saying to us in this House ad nauseam, and what we already know.
June 5, 1978

I want the minister and the government to address themselves, in spite of the fact that the taxpayers of Canada have provided 8,000 hopper cars since 1972, to the fact that our capacity to move grain by rail is less now than it was prior to the time we started providing hopper cars for the railroads.
The Minister of Transport, the government, this House, and the people of Canada have been misused and abused by the two national railway companies. In 1972 there were in excess of 26,000 railway cars available for grain movement. Since then we have provided 8,000 hopper cars, which is equivalent to 12,000 boxcars in grain movement; while the railways have taken 13,000 cars out of grain service; half of what there was in 1972. In other words, our capacity for moving grain by rail is not only no greater than what it was before we started supplying hopper cars but, I submit, our capacity is reduced. We have not increased the capacity of the grain handling system so far as rail transportation is concerned. We have not increased it to meet the expanded grain export objectives that the minister wants, the Wheat Board wants, and all of us want.
Why is there a backlog of 17 ships waiting to be loaded in Vancouver again this week? There is certainly no bottleneck in our country elevator system, and certainly our efficient farmers cannot be blamed for it. There is certainly no backlog in terms of the job which the Canadian Wheat Board is doing. It is doing the best job it can possibly do in the circumstances under which it has to operate, and the farmer-owned grain terminals are doing the best job they can, particularly on the west coast. In fact, west coast terminals could handle more grain to fill the boats than they are getting if the railroads were not dragging their feet.
I am sure the minister will tell us of the number of cars loaded and unloaded at Vancouver in March, April, and May. These are pretty good figures, but all they are doing is making up what they did not get done in November, December, January, and February. There are not enough railway cars to move the grain that we need in order to reduce, if not eliminate, the amount of time the ships wait in the ports. I do not suppose we could ever totally eliminate the waiting, but we could certainly substantially reduce it, this in spite of the fact that the taxpayers have provided the railways with 8,000 hopper cars.
As the federal government buys hopper cars for grain movement, the railways phase out their boxcars, so our capacity to move grain has not increased. We have "been had" by our two major railways, one publicly owned and one privately owned, and they are both guilty.
I will give you the exact figures, Mr. Speaker. Over 26,000 cars were available for grain movement at the end of 1972. By April of this year the number dropped to 15,200. By July 1 it will drop even further to 13,319 as a result of more cars which the railroads will remove from the grain service, which they are doing right at this moment.
Grain
By the end of this year the number of boxcars which the railroads have will be reduced to 12,083, and the projection of the railroads is that by 1981 they will only have 6,000 boxcars in grain movement. That might be a good deal for the railroads, but it is no bargain for the taxpayers, no bargain for the farmers, and certainly no bargain for the people who wish to buy our grain. What we need is a lot more control over the railroads to require them to provide adequate service.
The railroads cannot justify this, and I hope the minister will agree, because not only am I saying it but so are others outside of this place. The railways cannot justify refusing to supply adequate service to the grain industry because they claim to lose money on hauling grain. They, as utilities, are expected to provide service to all customers and to make money on an over-all basis. The valuable concessions and the large amounts of money, including the land grants that were given to the railroads at the beginning and the funds that have been given to them since then, are in exchange for the obligation that the railroads have to maintain sufficient rolling stock and locomotive power to meet the requirements of transportation in this country.
I hope the minister will not again try to make the excuse for the railroads that, because they are losing money on the movement of grain, they evade an obligation which they have to this country. It is not an excuse that we or anyone else can accept. We have provided tax write-off improvements in the last budget for the railroads, an additional 6 per cent on their rolling stock so that they can increase the amount of rolling stock they have.
What do the railroads do? Canadian Pacific Limited can spend $20 million on buying Syracuse China Corporation, in Syracuse, New York. Why did the minister or somebody else not direct them to put that $20 million into the purchase of more rolling stock? According to CPR's own statement, they are going to spend $50 million repairing 6,000 railway cars, but none of those cars are for grain movement. The minister is aware of this as much as I am or anyone else is.
I want to say that this does not apply to grain cars only. This is not a new problem. In 1947 there was a shortage of railway cars to move grain, but there was also, and there is still now, a shortage of stock cars. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) can tell you about that. The problem is chronic and continuous. In fact, when I attempted to move a motion under Standing Order 26, in ruling out the motion you said, Mr. Speaker, that the situation was chronic rather than acute, and you were perfectly right, sir.
Every year there are not enough cars to move potatoes out of the Atlantic provinces, not enough cars to move lumber out of British Columbia or northern Ontario, not enough stock cars to move livestock, and, most of all, not enough cars to move grain.
We say in our motion that the government has failed to expand Canada's capacity to move grain to export position, and while I recognize the contribution that the government and the people of Canada have made in their efforts to increase that capacity, it has been subverted and nullified by

June 5, 1978
Grain
the actions of the railways, because the minister and his government have failed to prevent the railroads from taking the wrong actions, and the minister and the government have thereby failed to expand our capacity, and that jeopardizes the ability of the Canadian Wheat Board to compete successfully and to expand our grain sales opportunities.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture is predicting that China in particular, and possibly the Soviet Union, will want additional grain over and above their present contracts, and the U.S. questions Canada's capacity to apply for, and successfully get, additional contracts because of the record of our railroads in the movement of grain.
We say in our motion that the minister and the government have failed to implement fully the major recommendations of the Hall commission report. I hate to say this because I do not mean it personally about the minister, but he is giving failure a bad name. If he will act upon the six items that we list in our motion, and if he will act on two or three others that I know my colleagues in my party and my colleagues to my right in the official opposition will point out, he will have the full support of this House. It will cost money, it will not be easy, and it will certainly require the government and parliament to make the two railroads perform better.
First, the minister should implement the recommendations of the Hall commission to maintain the statutory grain rates for producers and to pay directly to the railroads the actual difference between statutory and compensatory rates for grain transport. The minister bandied around the figure of $200 million to $250 million a year in the debate on this subject which took place approximately two or three weeks ago. 1 imagine he arrived at those figures by basing them on what Mr. Snavely recommended.
On behalf of my colleagues, I should like to indicate that what Mr. Snavely recommended was ridiculous and overly generous. Mr. Snavely proposed to build into compensatory rates for the railroads a 30 per cent return on equity investment or 20 per cent on the cost of capital. No self-respecting businessman or banker would ever talk in terms of a return of that nature. Not only is it greedy, but it is unconscionable. It sounds like something Household Finance or the lovey-dovey finance company would want. It is not a compensatory rate, it is a gift. The minister does not need to rely on the recommendations of Mr. Snavely in that regard.
If the Snavely formula were adopted, the railroads would receive 15 per cent more for hauling grain on an average than they would for hauling non-competitive other bulk commodities in the west. They would receive 27 per cent more per ton mile for hauling grain than they would receive on the average for hauling all other commodities in western Canada. I hope the minister is not considering allowing a compensatory rate for the grain companies on the basis of what Mr. Snavely recommends.
In our motion we refer to the actual difference between statutory and compensatory rates for grain transport which

should be paid directly to the railroads. Paragraph (b) reads as follows:
to implement the Hall commission recommendations on economic development by extending the statutory freight rate to other commodities in the prairies and to other regions;
Particularly we are referring to the Atlantic region. Then the same principle should apply. It takes into account our geography and climate. It takes into account where we can produce, manufacture, and process commodities in our respective regions. It takes into account the markets of the world and the need for an opportunity to compete in those markets.
Paragraph (c) is a follow up to paragraph (a). I hope the minister will take this paragraph into account. It reads as follows:
to require the railways to purchase 4,000 hopper cars and to repair and return a minimum of 5,000 box cars to grain movement;
We all know of the removal of thousands of boxcars from grain movement by the railroads, many of which were scrapped. Some of them were repaired and put into the movement of other kinds of merchandises such as furniture, newsprint or whatever. The minister was had. As and when hopper cars came on stream, railroads moved boxcars normally used for the movement of grain into the movement of other commodities. That was not good corporate citizenship on the part of CP or CN.
As the Premier of Saskatchewan and I have said, railroads cannot justify refusing to supply adequate service to the grain industry because they claim to be losing money. After the gifts, concessions, subsidies, funds and assistance from the federal government, as well as from the provinces and municipalities, they have no excuse.
Paragraph (d) reads as follows:
to reimburse the Canadian Wheat Board for costs of demurrage charges on ships delayed in loading through no fault of the producers or grain companies;
Since our grain exports, whether a record or a near record is set, are of benefit to the nation as a whole, and do wonders for our foreign exchange situation, our balance of payments, and our export situation, surely that paragraph in our motion is reasonable. Since grain exports are of benefit to the entire nation, surely the nation as a whole should pay this cost which is incurred through no fault of grain producers or grain companies. Not only are ships being delayed because of the inadequate number of railway cars, they are being delayed because of the inadequate use of facilities already in place. This morning I had a telephone conversation with the manager of a grain terminal in Vancouver. That terminal is cleaning and drying grain 24 hours a day. Also 16 hours a day are being spent unloading cars and loading ships.
The prairie provinces have five government elevators with a capacity of 17,100,000 bushels. As of today, slightly under four million bushels are stored in those terminals at Moose Jaw, Saskatoon, Edmonton, Calgary, and Lethbridge. Those five government elevators could be drying 50 to 100 carloads of grain a day. That grain could be delivered to Vancouver and would be ready for onship loading, unless it had to be cleaned.
June 5, 1978

In any case, there are facilities in the prairies which are not being used.
Mr. Justice Hall and his commission recommended the abolition of stopoff charges. Grain companies are not anxious to pay extra charges to stop cars off at Moose Jaw, Saskatoon or Edmonton. These charges, of course, come out of the pockets of farmers. They are not anxious to unload the grain at those points, dry it and reload it. Thus the grain is sent on to their own terminals which have limited drying capacity. At the moment large volumes of tough grain are arriving in Vancouver where it has to be dried before being loaded on to ships. Approximately 10 per cent or 15 per cent can be mixed with dry grain, but the rest of it is delayed in the terminals for the purpose of drying. The capacity for drying at the government elevators is not being used. I hope the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) will have something to say about that matter before this day is over.
Paragraph (e) of my motion reads as follows:
to increase immediately and substantially the amount of grain to be moved through the ports of Prince Rupert and Churchill;
For years we have known that the amount of grain going through Prince Rupert could be doubled with the existing facilities in trackage, storage space, loading and unloading capacities. The CN line to Prince Rupert is being used to about a 25 per cent capacity. Why are we not diverting some ships from Vancouver to Prince Rupert? Why are we not diverting rail cars of grain to Prince Rupert which are otherwise destined for Vancouver? A similar argument can be made in respect of Churchill. With the present facilities, the movement of grain through Churchill could be increased by at least five million bushels. The capacity at Prince Rupert could be increased by at least 20 million bushels with its existing facilities.
Why are not the Vancouver terminals operating three shifts a day, seven days a week? If that were done, those terminals would be faced with the same situation which occurred three or four years ago. The minister knows about that situation, as does the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) and myself. If the terminals called in shifts to work at midnight, enough cars are spotted to keep them working two or three hours, and then the workers must be sent home. Three shifts a day for several days a week are not feasible, unless and until a sufficient number of railway cars are spotted to keep them working.
I give credit to the minister, the government, the grain companies, and the Canadian Wheat Board for the efforts which have been made to date. But we are not keeping up, and we will not be able to make further gains unless the government or the minister requires the railroads to carry out the responsibilities and obligations that belong to them and to no one else.
I never thought for one moment that the railroads would use the provision of hopper cars as a means of reducing their own efforts. It was my belief they would remain good corporate
Grain
citizens and carry on to the capacity they had before we started providing hopper cars. I am not aware of any purchases by the railroads of rolling stock for grain movement as a result of the new budget provisions. I know of no railway funds that are to go into the purchase of cars for hauling grain.
When I mentioned this chronic shortage of rolling stock for a number of commodities, and the minister knows this as well as I, I had in mind that hopper cars for grain had helped the situation, but there was also a problem in respect of a shortage of hopper cars for the movement of potash. At one point in time the railways were running a thousand cars per month behind for the movement for potash.
On the other hand we have heard reports, and one or two of my colleagues will be going into this in greater detail, that hopper cars suitable for the movement of potash are sitting idly on sidings. They could be cleaned and used for grain. Many of these cars are owned by private companies for leasing. The minister should give the Canadian Wheat Board the money to clean these cars up and put them into the movement of grain. We have only one and a half months left of this crop year in which the minister can take further action.
If the projections of the United States Department of Agriculture are accurate, we are going to be in real trouble by November. That country will be picking up additional sales that we could otherwise have obtained if we had increased our capacity to move grain by rail.
I have tried not to harp at or nag the minister on the subject of arguments we have had on many other occasions. We have tried in this motion to make some positive proposals and suggestions. We have said to him that we support his efforts, the efforts of the government and of the Canadian Wheat Board, particularly in the provision of hopper cars and the job the Board has done in obtaining grain sales. Surely the minister should listen to and accept what we are saying in a positive manner about increasing our ability to transport grain to our export positions. This really should be done by the railroads.
The situation would improve if the minister implemented the Hall commission recommendations regarding rates. Never mind buying all the recommendations of Snavely. This would not cost much more, and perhaps not as much as it is presently costing the government in the purchase of hopper cars, as well as the funding for other purposes. By implementing the Hall recommendations the railroads would be required not only to purchase the rolling stock and repair what they now have, it would require them to do their own rebuilding of the branch lines, instead of the taxpayer having to put up the money in a different way. Given the difference between the statutory rate and a reasonable compensatory rate, they could be required to do the job which, after all, is theirs to do. It is not up to the minister or an agency such as the Canadian Wheat Board to bail the railroads out of trouble continually, while the railroads run off into other more lucrative fields, both in and outside this country.
It is time we required the railroads to accept their responsibilities and carry out their obligations. They have been unfair to the Minister of Transport, who is also in charge of the

June 5, 1978
Grain
Wheat Board. They have misused and abused him, as well as the grain producers of this country. They have misused and abused the Canadian Wheat Board. They have placed our dealings with nations which are considering buying more grain from us in jeopardy. Surely it is time for the minister and the government to kick those two outfits around and make them produce. If the minister does that he will have the support of members on all sides of this House, as well as of the farmers, farm organizations, and the Canadian Wheat Board.
And even the NFU.

Yes, and even the NFU. They might even starting talking again.
I appreciate that the final paragraph of this motion contains a bone of contention so far as this party, the government, and the official opposition are concerned. However, if the minister would accept and implement the other points, this would improve the situation immensely.
I hope the minister will accept my suggestions to increase grain movement capacity. In this way the terminals in Vancouver would receive less tough grain because more of it would be dried in government elevators on the prairies. We could enable the terminals to go on three shifts a day, six or seven days a week, unloading grain cars and loading ships. Some of the ships could be diverted to Prince Rupert where they could be loaded. I am sure some of this would not make the Wheat Pools and the grain companies happy, but that is just too bad. We have to get the job done. I hope the minister will accept and consider these positive and objective proposals, and will act accordingly. He does not have much time. We have been arguing about this since last November.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) made an announcement last Friday that there is to be a special investigation into grain movement. I do not know why the minister did not make the announcement. Good God, how many more do we need? The minister has access to more figures than do I, and he knows the ones I have given him. He does not need another investigation. I hope he will take hold of this in a stronger way than he has in the past. He need not argue with myself or the hon. member for Vegreville. He can, if he wishes, and we will enjoy it. He should get into a winning fight with management, the board of directors and the operating personnel of the railroads so that we can accomplish what we are aiming for in the motion.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to begin by dealing with one of the last paragraphs included in the motion of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) because it does not really fit consistently with the picture created by the other parts of his recommendations dealing with transportation and the Hall commission report. I refer to his suggestion that marketing of certain feed grains rapeseed, flax, and rye, be placed under the board.
When referring to this paragraph the hon. member acknowledged that he was reaching a little beyond the scope of the rest

of his motion. He said it probably would not sit very well with the government or the official opposition, at which point the critic of the official opposition across the floor was heard to say "nor with the farmers". This is because included in the motion is a reference to rapeseed, in respect of which a plebiscite was held among farmers to determine their wishes. In allowing rapeseed to be marketed as it had been marketed before the plebiscite, we are simply following the expressed wishes of the farmers. At the very most I might have thought the hon. member would suggest that the time was ripe for further consultation with the farmers, rather than simply to presume to override their wishes recently expressed in a plebiscite.
I was delighted to get the advice from the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre that I should not refer to the fact that we are having a record year for export, with improved prospects for meeting the transportation challenge with which we are faced at the present time. I am sure he would like me to avoid any reference to that, because for some days he and some of his negative friends have managed to leave the impression about the country that everything is in a disastrous state. The fact of a record being moved does not exactly fit into that picture, so he would prefer me to be silent about it.
In the same way, the second last paragraph of the motion contains the following suggestion:
to increase immediately and substantially the amount of grain to be moved through the ports of Prince Rupert and Churchill:
I presume he includes that paragraph by way of congratulations to the government for doing exactly that, although being in the New Democratic Party it would not be his ordinary practice to extend congratulations-so he puts it in the negative form.
Just today a telegram came to my hand from Dr. Hick, chairman of the grain co-ordinating committee in Prince Rupert containing congratulations for the government. He says that our continued commitment to the port is much appreciated, and he notes a tremendous volume of grain being moved through Prince Rupert this year.
In the same way I have said to the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith)-who continues to sound off negatively about that port when he asks questions with dismay-that once again this year, and likely for the third year in a row, we will notch up the amount of grain moving through Churchill. It may not seem to be a great deal when we just edge up the volume, but it means that in each of these last three years, and this year again, I predict, if things go at all half decently, we will set another record in Churchill. That will be the third record in a row.
In the case of Churchill, previous to this we have announced various expenditures of $5 million to $7 million for improving to capacity the state of the elevator and the state of the harbour, in our continued commitment to the port. We have also announced, as part of our rebuilding program of rail lines, the commitment of the money to add a couple of sidings to the
June 5, 1978

Herchmer subdivision and, in effect, to increase greatly the capacity of that line to carry grain to Churchill. This would mean that we could go after a further record in the following years, although the construction itself will take some time.
There we have our commitment and our constant improvements in the way in which we use these two important northern ports.
In Prince Rupert, of course, in addition to setting very high levels of exports this year, we have indicated our willingness to support, financially, the improvements in the port. My colleague, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), is at work on improvements to the existing grain terminal there to increase its capacity and ability to handle grain. Along with a variety of elevator companies, we are hoping to be in a position to ensure the construction of a major additional terminal facility in the port of Prince Rupert designed to handle the increased volume of grain which we see, in our optimism, in the years ahead.
I say in our optimism, Mr. Speaker, because when I say that this is a record year for the movement of grain into export, and that we expect to set another record and surpass the other two times in our history when we exceeded 800 million bushels of exports of grain and grain products, the significance is not just in the fact that it is a record on its own, but that in this volume of 810 million to 850 million bushels of grain-and with the lower figure plus grain products-we are moving into export effectively more than a mere record or record crop or the part of that crop which is available for export.
In 1976 and in 1977 prairie grain farmers produced the best two crops in our history, yet with the 1977 crop which is close to the record of 1976, when we export 800 to 850 million bushels, we will be moving the whole of the available grain from that crop plus a significant amount from the previous crop, and that was available because it also was such a record.
I am optimistic about the future, and about these production levels being repeated more frequently and not simply standing as records for a long time. For that reason we want to build and expand the system. We will be looking to every technique we know to improve the system and its capability of handling grain to export.
The development of Prince Rupert, eventually to be able to handle perhaps 150 million bushels of grain in a year by 1982, in my view is consistent with a target of perhaps one billion bushels of export within a year or so of that time.
The problem we have in finding enough equipment and terminal capacity to handle grain is the problem of finding that capacity when we are moving an amount we never moved before. How much capacity should we have on hand to move a crop or handle a product? I know that no one would be satisfied if we only had enough capacity to move an average crop in a year. That would mean that any year we were above average we would be restrained from seizing markets by moving that additional production.
It is also obvious that as you have capacity, whether in railway cars, freight lines or terminals, to move more than the
Grain
average amount of grain being produced, then you have some of that equipment sitting idle in a certain and significant number of years. The economic question that always has to be asked is how much we should have on hand, and how much we should be able to move. The point is that in receiving from producers, perhaps for the first time in history, one billion bushels of grain, we are testing the system to the full.
As the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre said, a great deal of the credit for the fact that we are testing the system goes to the Canadian Wheat Board. I was happy that he gave some credit to the government. I think it is deserved in terms of the credit facilities provided and the encouragement given to the Wheat Board to go out and sell. Not long ago, Mr. Jarvis, the chief commissioner, said that one of the objectives, one of the ways of going about marketing, is to push the system to the full. The other way would have been to tailor sales to a comfortable margin of ability to handle. He said in effect they chose the route of pushing the system to the full.
I should like hon. members to know that last fall when the Canadian Wheat Board asked me about their willingness and desire to go in that direction, I was full of encouragement even though I knew there would likely be tightness in the system and problems of ships waiting, as there have been in years gone by when less grain was moved.
Not long ago I saw a clipping dated February, 1961, when the Conservative party was in power. In those years we never got close to 500 million bushels of exports, yet this clipping bemoaned the fact that great numbers of ships were in Vancouver waiting to load.
This negativism on the part of hon. members is unfortunate for the country as a whole. I am sure it sometimes leaves a bad impression in the minds of our buyers. Perhaps it should be put into the context that the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool put it in during a radio report not long ago. They pointed out that the fact of ships waiting is not an uncommon thing in the world of shipping. On May 19, according to their calculations, in the gulf and in the United States nine ships were loading, and 39 ships were waiting; in Argentina 45 ships were waiting in three separate ports. A waiting period of 15 to 20 days was common, according to the report. This is as long or longer than the few worst days in our recent period of ships being delayed.
Many others have explained that the world of shipping is not a regular one and that delays, and therefore demurrage, are an expected part of a rapid movement of product, particularly when we are, as now, setting a record.
We have done many things to improve the system and to improve our ability to handle grain. When those who want to be negative speak about the decline in the number of boxcars, ignoring the purchase of hopper cars which are worth one and one-half boxcars each, they are being misleading. They further ignore the fact that we have gained in efficiency by getting a better turn-around time for boxcars and hopper cars-that by appointing co-ordinators at Thunder Bay and Vancouver, by the introduction of the block shipping system, with the hopper cars themselves and their more efficient handling and breaking system, with the agreement we were finally able to work out

June 5, 1978
Grain
between the railways so that cars no longer pass one another loaded, going north and south between Edmonton and Calgary but instead were exchanged by the railways at those points and went directly to port-that these things have created improvements and helped shorten the turn-around time, which means that we can handle more grain like the record we are doing this year with less equipment than would have been required a few years ago. We are not resting there.
We have a branch line rebuilding program. Obviously, in addition to creating certainty throughout the province about branch lines that will be there and in operation for many years to come, this will allow cars to be moved more quickly onto them and off them. Therefore it will again lower the amount of time to be spent by a car on that line.
We have mainline improvements which will likewise improve our system. Some of these are again the direct result of government action. I think particularly of the developments which are taking place on the mainline of the Canadian Pacific Railway through the Rockies. These were brought about because of budget changes which allowed faster write-off of those sorts of investments, because we could see on the analysis that was given to us that the cash flow of the railway would not have induced it to make those improvements without that change. Those changes will lower the incline of lines, improve capacity, double track the lines, and improve our chances of getting the better turnaround.
The improvements at Prince Rupert and in the Herchimer subdivision are other examples of what will expedite movement of cars.
So, the question is, how many cars should we have? There is no secret that we are looking now, as we did on three occasions in the past, at the question of when cars will be required, whether boxcars should be rehabilitated, more new hopper cars purchased, or whether we should go forward with some combination of those things.
We have the cars today to handle the 850 million-bushel record which was our target for this year. With the problems of delays during the winter, it became very tight to do that, and we may not quite achieve that total. We need more cars for the prospective movement, the prospective replacement of cars that are gradually dying because of their age, and the growth production, which 1 foresee and the Wheat Board and I believe in as a reality, and for which we want to provide for by investment in cars as well as terminal facilities to handle the needs of the future.
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre said that we have failed to implement fully the major recommendations of the Hall commission report. Members opposite have said so many times too. I have asked them to give me a document, or to document in their speeches which recommendations it is they want us to implement faster than we have been doing, how they want them implemented and whether they want them implemented, even if the consensus of the Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta pools is against particular recommen-

dations, and likewise the grain industry and farm organizations generally.
In that regard I refer to the question of whether to set up an operating rail authority called the prairie rail authority where we have the support of all of these organizations in not moving in that direction but instead seizing that part of the recommendation from the Hall commission report to create a western arm of the Canadian Transport Commission to deal with future branch lines and the conditions under which the railways will operate them. So far as I know, every significant farm organization in the west supports that course of action and supports the setting up of the prairie rail action committee because what the railways wanted, what the farm community needed was certainty about that remaining 2,000 miles of line which were left uncertain as to their long-term future by the Hall commission report.
We have implemented the major recommendations. We have transferred to the basic rail network the 1,813 miles recommended by the commission. Not a mile has been changed in that regard. We then moved immediately to begin the rebuilding of those lines.
Here I would like to refer to a few other recommendations, and the only ones to which the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre refers. He says that we have failed to implement the Hall commission report by-what does he say-not taking the following action: He wants us to take this action and says, "Implement the Hall commission report and the recommendation to maintain the statutory grain rates for producers". We have done so. We have maintained the statutory grain rate for producers. Then he says, "and pay directly to the railways the difference between the statutory and compensatory rates". In saying that we have one authority on what that difference was, and that was the Snavely report. He immediately rushes forward and says that he does not think we should rely on that. We presumably need another analysis and another report to satisfy him. I am not altogether sure that I would go along with the final figures of the Snavely report either, particularly because the Snavely report itself points out a couple of areas where serious judgment would have to be exercised.
I agree with the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre that the appropriate return on capital would have to be looked at very carefully in any final analysis. The member for Regina-Lake Centre wants us and urges us to pay the difference to the railways. He says that he does not know what the difference is, but we should pay it. If we did pay it and had paid it quickly, he would have screamed "gift" from one end of the country to the other, But he says pay the difference to the railways, if we can figure out what it is.
What did we do? We moved on two specific fronts first, in the purchase of hopper cars with the provision of $255 million worth of railway equipment for moving grain; secondly in a repair program for rebuilding cars a couple of years ago, which he may ignore; and now in the specific program of rebuilding branch lines where there can be no argument about whether this is too much or not enough for the railways. In 1977-1978 we put in $100 million for rebuilding. We had a
June 5, 1978

full and detailed agreement which specified the equipment which was to be purchased with that money, $47 million worth. Why? Because the railways needed more ballast cars to carry the gravel and crushed rock. They needed more equipment such as the sleds to lift the lines, and more dump cars, in other words, more of the equipment than they had to rebuild the lines because of course the regular rebuilding and repair programs had to go on. As well there were $53 million dollars more for specific and on-line improvements such as you now see on the Conquest subdivision through Beechy and Lucky Lake in Saskatchewan which, in the next few years, we will see in terms of ballast and improved road beds and improved lines throughout the prairie region. Some $75 million a year has now been committed through the railways for that very specific purpose. Dollar for dollar we are getting value in improved rail lines.
Whether the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre could argue that we are giving the railways too much if we adopted the Snavely report, or not enough if we adopted another figure, I say to him that at least he should be able to accept that when we are buying hopper cars, which he agrees are needed-he, unlike Mr. Hall in a recent news report, agreed that buying hopper cars was a good thing and still is a good thing- whether we give the $100 million to the railways and then demand they buy hopper cars and make them available to the railway, this is not a matter of great fiscal moment nor a moment too soon in regard to the handling of our grain.
It is the purchasing and acquiring of that equipment which is important. At least when we put our money into the hopper cars and make sure that every dollar goes into them, and we put our money into the rebuilding of branch lines and make sure every dollar goes into them, there can hardly be an argument that a dollar is being misspent and benefiting the railways unduly.
I calculate that today even taking a fairly modest view of the Snavely figures, it would require, taking the 1974 figures and updating them, something over $100 million a year in addition to the branch line subsidy amount to compensate the railways for moving grain. We are providing $70 million this year and $75 million next year for cash for branch line rebuilding. Surely hon. members opposite would not want that program to go more slowly. Indeed, the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) said at one point it should go more quickly. The unions which were to be working on that repair program urged me to take just that kind of time over it. They do not want to see a great surge of building and then idle capacity while rebuilding lines, which would occur if you build and rebuild them in a hurry. It does not make economic sense to rush in that fashion.
What we have been doing is identifying lines. I could go through the lists of the hundreds of thousands of miles of line which are going to be improved throughout Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Manitoba during the course of 1978, and identify the additional schedules for the years to come.
Grain
Therefore, in effect we maintain the Crow rate. We have paid to the railways a very large part of the difference between that rate and the cost of carrying grain through our hopper car purchase programs, our rebuilding programs, and by our indication of our belief in going in that direction and making sure that the grain handling system is in order.
The hon. member says the next thing we should do in the Hall commission report is to implement the recommendation on economic development by extending the statutory freight rate to other commodities in the prairies. He does add "and to other regions".
The Crow rate is a traditional rate of the prairie farmer. I have always seen it as a classic offset against the tariff system, which has not helped him but hurt him in his costs, while he sells in an international world. I have said time and again that I would fight to maintain the benefit of the Crow rate for the prairie farmer so long at least as the tariff system exists.
I think, and farm leaders seem to agree with me, that if we can move toward freer trade, there would be a bargain one could strike, and the Crow rate would be thrown into that bargain because the farmer would be much better off by freer trade than he is from the benefit of the Crow. That aside, since we are a long way from that by any sign in the world and where it is going, the Crow rate is a traditional benefit. It now represents in today's cost terms approximately $200 million in this year, $200 million that has to be supplied, even according to Hall, and endorsed by members opposite, to the railways or through the railways by the government.
That is the $100 million I referred to earlier, plus the branch line subsidies, which is effectively part and parcel of the same program. That $200 million a year commitment will be ongoing from the people of Canada in relation to the Crow rate.
The Hall commission has said, "extend that to other products." I am not sure the commission said "in other regions". Perhaps that is a little addition by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre. He acknowledges it is. I am glad to see his logic, at least in being bold enough to say this.
I would like the Conservatives in their turn to analyse how far they would go in this payment of compensation in lower rates on other products. I presume that while the Crow rate applies only on grain moving to Thunder Bay, Vancouver, or the west coast for export, it would be very difficult not to extend any rate that was lowered in relation to meat and other products to the domestic market on the west coast as well as to export. It would be very hard politically not to do that.
It would be very difficult not to extend the lower rate in some other form of subsidization to anything that moved by way of truck as well as by rail or, indeed, any other method of transportation. Therefore, we would extend it to the movement of all products, at least to Thunder Bay, Vancouver and the west coast generally.
Then I would ask about whether that rate would have to be applied in some system of justice to those products moving

June 5, 1978
Grain
shorter distances within the country, stopping at Edmonton, Calgary, Thunder Bay or any place in the east.
I ask the opposition as well, would they extend that lower rate on truck and rail, and then water presumably, to every movement of product, such as grain, meat and other products, wherever it is in the country, or would they defend a lower rate on meat in one region of the country and for a similar distance in another region?
If I put all of those things together, by political calculation and by political analysis of what would be required eventually because of complaints from other regions, quite justified, I would not be surprised to come up with a figure of another $200 million a year for those lower freight rates. Indeed, it could be a good deal higher than that. Therefore, we would be asking the treasury to add to the $200 million a year, of which $100 million is a brand new commitment, another $200 million.
In addition, they would defeat another recommendation of the Hall commission report which is that production should occur according to natural advantage. In taking a real cost like the freight of moving a product, and either eliminating it or lowering it, you encourage the shipment of the more bulky form of that product farther than would be the case if you leave the rates at their natural or real cost level.
The very existence of such a subsidy program would make it less likely than the reflecting of real costs through to the person shipping the product, that he compacts his barley into meat before he moves it on any great distance. The over-riding question, of course, is the cost which would be involved in doing this and the burden upon the treasury which would be built into the system. I say it will be difficult to justify this burden upon the treasury.
I know there will be spokesmen from the Conservative party who are from the west, and also from the New Democratic Party, who will say quietly that this will be a great thing and not worry too much about the question of how far they would have to extend it into other regions. As a spokesman for the official opposition, I would like the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) to make clear it is the official policy of his party. I would like to see that said by his leader some time. His leader, of course, may want to backtrack on that at a later date. He has said that he would like to have the wheat board competed with in international markets by the international traders. I am not sure whether all of his colleagues go along with him on that. He may not have known what he said, although he is an Alberta boy. In any event, I would like to know whether that is the official policy of the party. I would like to see them spell out step by step what is included. Then I would like to see them explain whether it would be an advantage or not-

Mr. Speaker, we in the Progressive Conservative party welcome debate on this motion at this time. As has been pointed out by previous speakers, the motion is fairly comprehensive. It has many facets.
I have to agree with the minister when he observes that paragraph (/), which has to do with the orderly marketing and returning of marketing of feed grains to the sole jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board, is really not very compatible with
June 5, 1978

the thrust of the motion. I can agree with the minister's summation in that regard, but that is about as far as I can go, because once again he is attempting to leave the impression that all is well, things could be worse.
Quite frankly, I find little reason to be optimistic in listening very carefully to what the minister had to say. In spite of what he said, this debate comes at the height of a very serious and major breakdown in our grain handling and transportation capacity. Right now in the port of Vancouver we have something like 20 or more ships waiting, and ten in Thunder Bay. Our country elevator system is plugged. Producers are up in arms. We have a 35 million or 36 million bushel shortfall in our anticipated target. There is a shortage of equipment. There are severe cutbacks in the available number of boxcars and hopper cars in the country elevator system. Demurrage costs are piling up.
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) seemed to lay the total blame on the railroads. The grain carrying fleet is being reduced at a dramatic pace. In addition something like 23,000 CN cars are away in the United States compared with 13,000 as a normal average over the year. These figures were given to us by the president of the Transport Commission on Thursday last. He went on to say that these cars were being used on a no-charge basis for the transportation of goods in the United States. Surely the minister has some authority over an organization which is, after all, a Crown corporation. Surely there must be some means by which these boxcars can be brought back to Canada and used to transport our grain.
The appointment of a tribunal to inquire immediately into certain aspects of prairie grain handling facilities by the hon. gentleman's colleague, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale), contradicts what the minister has been saying. It proves that a serious problem exists. Yet the minister has the audacity to stand up here and tell us everything is fine. It is a deplorable situation, and it is well summed up in the comments made by a couple of members of the unions involved. This is what a Canadian Press report on the subject had to say:
Canada will lose its foreign grain markets if the federal government doesn't smarten up and make sure the grain is delivered to waiting ships, Henry Kanes, head of the Grain Workers Union said Friday ...
Dennis McDermott, president of the Canadian Labour Congress, said in a news release that the railways have failed to deliver grain to the ports for export and that "the credibility of Canada in world grain trade is endangered and demurrage fees on ships waiting to load grain in Vancouver could approach $17 million ..
McDermott said the federal government should not have allowed the deterioration of railway boxcar fleets.
"The government has known for a long time there would be heavy shipments but it has done nothing to increase capacity" McDermott said, following a meeting earlier in the week of a CLC grain-handling committee.
Kanes and McDermott said if Canada loses its export markets for grain "major ports and other sections of the grain-handling system will face major lay-offs..
Those are not statements by members of the opposition. Those are not statements by people engaging in a parade of
Grain
negativism. These are views expressed by people who are deeply concerned about the ability of this country to discharge its responsibilities and meet its commitments. They are anxious Canada should maintain its credibility as a reliable supplier of grain.
This situation should be considered against the background of the Liberal election promises in 1974 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) promised that a Liberal government would "revamp the grain handling system from the granaries to the ships in the harbour."
Today's debate comes at a time when the government must make some serious decisions about the Hall report. It must decide either to put up or shut up. It cannot continue to say that it favours the report, while at the same time subverting, twisting, and undermining the central recommendations of the report.
Hear, hear!

The Hall report is not only a transportation charter, it is an economic manifesto for Western Canada. It is not enough to implement some of the recommendations, those which are easy to put in place, such as rail line abandonment, those which result in reduced services for customers and pressures upon the producer. The minister should not implement the less attractive features of the report without moving toward the adoption of the entire package. I listened very carefully to the minister and found him very defensive on this subject. I heard what he had to say about the basic network. He did not come clean on this issue. I say you cannot adopt one part of the report without the other, without adopting those recommendations which tend to compensate and offset those less attractive features. The Hall recommendations must be considered as a total package.
The minister has told us the government is moving in some areas. There is no doubt that with regard to certain of the recommendations it is moving quickly, indeed with indecent haste. In this process the interests of the producers are being forgotten though the interests of the railroads and the grain companies are being given consideration. As I have indicated, a number of the recommendations are very beneficial, and it is [DOT] these which the government is implementing only very slowly when it is not ignoring them entirely. Yet I believe these latter recommendations are part of a catalyst which could revolutionize grain handling and transportation.
The continual conflict between the minister and Mr. Justice Emmett Hall must be resolved. I hope that the proceedings in our committee will help bring the two parties together. In spite of the minister's kicking and screaming because he did not want Mr. Justice Hall to appear before the committee-
Oh!

I understand that the minister met with Mr. Justice Emmett Hall for the first time last Saturday, for the first time, I suspect, since the report was released more than a year ago.

June 5, 1978
Grain
There is in this country a tremendous amount of confidence in Mr. Justice Hall. He has been appointed commissioner in a contract dispute involving the western grain industry. Those people have confidence in him. The farmers have confidence in him. The people of western Canada have confidence in him. The only person who does not have confidence in him is the minister. If the hon. gentleman did feel confidence in him, Mr. Justice Hall would be free to come before the committee and state his case.
