speechtext: He is coming before the committee.
Against the minister's wishes.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext: I appointed the commission.

I commend the minister for that. I commend the work the commission did. They did a thorough and comprehensive job. And I wish the minister would not treat the gentleman and his colleagues with the contempt he has shown them in the past.
Many of us feel the minister has failed to grasp the real significance of these recommendations. He has told us he set out immediately to transfer those 1,800 miles to the basic network. But there are other areas which are far more important to the future of transportation and economic development in western Canada. It is about time the minister got on to the same wavelength as the authors of this report.
Now we have another commission, with a new set of recommendations. Then we have the Snavely report which, in many cases, challenges the major recommendations of the Hall report. In fact, it challenges the major recommendation regarding payment to the railways by the public treasury of the difference between the statutory rate and a fair compensatory rate. Clearly, the government will have to make up its mind as to which royal commission it is going to follow. Whose recommendations will the government adopt? I think that is very important.
No doubt Snavely is an expert in the field of freight rates, and I would be the last to argue with his findings. I understand that his statistics and figures are reasonably accurate, but his conclusions are another matter. I would much rather accept the conclusions of Mr. Hall than those of Mr. Snavely. Quite frankly, I do not believe that anyone can measure with any degree of accuracy the social and economic impact of the Crow rate and the impact of extension of that Crow rate sitting in a board room in the city of Washington.
Quite frankly, I place my credence in the recommendations of Mr. Hall. He knows the west. He has visited practically every community in western Canada. He has talked to the people, to the grain companies and to the transportation companies, and he really understands not only the problems but also the social and economic impact of any major deviation or change in the transportation system.

What has been the response of the government to the Hall recommendations? The minister has said that the government has acted decisively and quickly. I agree that in some areas it has. It has done so where it has been advantageous to the government and probably to the railways and grain handling companies. However, our analysis suggests that less than ten recommendations have been fully or partially implemented. There are some 90 recommendations in the Hall report. Fifty-eight have not been implemented at all. There has been no action on them. Statements have been made on 24. Six have been fully implemented, and four partially. That is not a very good record.
I said earlier that the minister did designate 1,813 miles into the basic network. He is proceeding with 2,165 miles of abandonment. However, with respect to the 2,344 miles put into that uncertain category there is a major deviation from the Hall report in the method which the government has adopted. There is a major deviation in the method of the government and in its timing, because we find that the minister is insisting on proceeding on the category with undue haste. I say that time is required to determine the status of these lines. Time is required to determine what kind of rationalization or consolidation will take place as far as grain-handling companies are concerned. The requirements of 1977 might be quite different from the requirements of 1985, so Mr. Justice Emmett Hall recommended a prairie rail authority which could monitor and run these lines.
1 am not suggesting that a prairie rail authority would be the be all and end all, but something like that certainly is necessary. I might say that this seemed to have widespread support from grain companies and from the railways. The government has proceeded with setting up a prairie rail action committee and, quite frankly, it is moving ahead very swiftly. The minister wants the committee to report back on the status of these lines by the end of this year. There does not seem to be the kind of consultation that is necessary. The producers are frustrated and very concerned.
I have in my hand a letter from Kelwood, Manitoba. It is from a Mr. George Carr, who is the secretary-treasurer of the Neepawa-McCreary Branch Lines Association. He indicates that an official report has been received from the Railway Transport Committee regarding applications for the abandonment of certain branch lines in Manitoba. This includes the line on which two of that association's elevators are situated, the Neepawa Junction to Rossburn Junction line, 32.8 miles. Should this be implemented there would be no elevator between Neepawa and McCreary, a distance of 40 miles. Mr. Carr felt that this decision was far too abrupt. The lines association wrote to the CTC in Ottawa last August regarding some of its concerns, and the reply it received stated that no line could be closed without a public hearing. It is now found that this line is finished, and much frustation has been created. To say the least, it has been very disconcerting to the producers who are affected.
Regarding rehabilitation, Mr. Hall said that an adequate network configuration will require capital funding of about
June 5, 1978

$445 million for upgrading and rehabilitation. The government responded, first, by committing $200 million, but it backed off and said that because of fiscal restraint it had to cut that back to $100 million.
That has since been supplemented by $75 million which is part of an additional $600 million program over five or ten years, I am not sure which.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext: Eight.

The minister says it is eight years. In the meantime the railways are committing additional expenditures. CN says it will commit at least $200 million over the next five years. It should. We just wrote off $808 million by way of a bill in this House. That bill will provide CN with a profit well in excess of $200 million by 1981. CP is also proposing expenditures to upgrade and rehabilitate its lines. The budget proposals should assist, but the $600 million seems to us to be more than generous, particularly when we consider that we do not seem to have adequate commitments and safeguards, when we see the railways reducing their grain-carrying fleet, and particularly when we see we have no control over the cars that go to the United States.
This ad hoc approach that we have bothers us very much, and I think that Justice Emmett Hall may have had the right idea: pay the railways a fair return for hauling grain, and charge them with the responsibility of maintaining their track and their infrastructure. Charge them with the responsibility of providing sufficient equipment and rolling stock.
I now turn to the Crow rate and the extension of the Crow rate. These two sections are very central to the thrust of the Hall report. They are very important to western Canada. Mr. Justice Emmett Hall said that the railways must be compensated for the cost of moving grain by rail and that the railways must in turn be responsible for maintenance and upgrading of lines in the basic network or those lines subsequently added to it. Mr. Justice Hall went on to say that the present statutory rates should be retained and that the shortfall between the cost of moving grain and the statutory rates should be paid directly to the railways. Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take part in the discussion on the motion of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). Naturally, I will not repeat all the terms of the motion and I will simply say that it concerns the lack of co-ordination among various government agencies. They are the Canadian Wheat Board, the Canadian Transportation Commission and the Canadian National Railways. These various agencies simply do not have the same objectives as concerns the economic development of our country.
Grain
The motion of my colleague for Regina-Lake Centre notes first of all chaos which surrounds rail transport in Canada. And yet it took the railroads to save Confederation and achieve the Canadian union. The motion states with reason that the government has not seen fit to promote the expansion of Canada's capacity to move grain to export positions thereby reducing our foreign sales opportunities.
Everyone knows that our railway system has become somewhat outmoded. Indeed, on October 26, 1974, I proposed a motion in the House of Commons to study the need to institute a royal inquiry commission concerning the well known deficiency of the Canadian National Railways in relation with the many deficits and the high number of accidents in the Canadian National system. As concerns the deficits, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian National has accumulated each year for nearly 20 years phenomenal deficits that the Canadian people must pay with their taxes.
In this 20 year period, the deficits accumulated by the Canadian National have reached $675 million, while the Canadian Pacific, which provides services in nearly the same areas, has had benefits often in excess of $100 million a year. And, as far as I know, in relation with the high number of accidents in the CN system, both as concerns costly derailments and employee safety, nothing has been done to correct the situation.
Mr. Speaker, it is impossible for me to ignore the very stern comments of coroner Heroux about the CN following the death of a CN employee in disturbing circumstances. On that occasion, it had been impossible to submit a report drafted by CN policemen and I still maintain that it is essential to launch a public inquiry on the CN administration. The purpose of such inquiry would be to investigate promotions and expenditures in the CN.
It is sad, Mr. Speaker, to note how the CN has for some ten years neglected its passenger services, so that it was necessary to reorganize recently those services within the framework of VIA Rail. As for freight, the CN has never been an innovator. We should be looking at what has been done in European countries where immediately after the war modern and rapid railways were developed.
In short, our railroads are in a pitiful condition. Instead of indulging in second class operations like building communication towers and commercial centres and owning real estate like luxury hotels, railways should commit themselves to maintaining adequate facilities and services as well as an appropriate number of freight cars and engines and, particularly they should develop new lines where it is required for our economic welfare.
Mr. Speaker, in the last four years, many questions have been put and many motions have been presented to the effect that railways in western Canada were not maintaining decent services for grain and cattle transportation from west to east. In the last report of the Canadian Wheat Board the growth

JuneS, 1978
Grain
rate of operations is said to have increased by 11 per cent at Churchill and 12 per cent at Prince Rupert. Those figures are encouraging as concerns the development of our secondary harbours.
I am particularly interested in the third part of the motion. It requires that CN and CP buy 4,000 hopper cars and return a minimum of 5,000 boxcars to grain movement. I think this request tells much about the present situation. We must improve it immediately and see to the maintenance of the rolling stock and the building of additional cars as needed. The efforts made until now to modernize the system have been certainly inadequate. Let us take again as an example the passenger train service. The public has been complaining about it for several decades. Pressure groups have been formed. Following the establishment of VIA Rail not much has been done and the bus and airlines companies are getting the major part of that market. However, VIA Rail is a step in the right direction. The creation of that company has made possible the redirection of railways towards passenger services.
As far as freight is concerned, it might be more realistic to create a joint corporation similar to VIA Rail that would include freight services of both railway companies. Then we would make sure that the economic interest of our country override private interests. It would be easier to redirect railways development in Canada to facilitate better services throughout our country.
My colleague for Regina-Lake Centre has given us a great opportunity by presenting his motion. It allows us to reflect seriously on the future of our railways and the development of our economy.

Mr. Speaker, I also would like to participate in this very important debate. In the 1974 election campaign the Liberal government promised many times to overhaul the entire grain transportation system. In fact, it promised $1.5 billion to be spent on transportation. Since that time very little has happened. Our system of moving grain to export, which is one of the major revenue sources for this country, is in serious trouble.
What are the signs of trouble that we see at present? There are three main signs which we have been seeing in the past few months. The first sign was when China, one of our major customers, started complaining that they were not getting the proper kind of service. As a result they turned to the United States for the first time in a number of years for additional purchases of grain.
The second sign of trouble which was apparent to most people was when the Canadian Wheat Board wanted action taken on its request for hopper cars and asked for a program for rebuilding of boxcars. That does not happen very often, Mr. Speaker, but it happened some months ago.

The third sign of trouble, which was perhaps the most obvious sign, was given last Friday when a Liberal backbencher made a press statement in his home town stating that a special and immediate investigation will be carried out into the efficient use of the prairie grain handling and transportation facilities. That was a true sign of trouble for this government and for the hon. member who made the statement.
Why is the industry in trouble? The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in his speech glossed over the problems which the industry is having. What is the situation of the industry at present? As of June 1, last Friday to be exact, we had 7 ships on the west coast loading, 17 ships waiting, and 17 more ships due, for a total of 401,000 tons waiting to be loaded. In Thunder Bay, we had 6 ships loading, 18 ships waiting, and 8 more due, for a total of 185,000 tons. In the St. Lawrence ports, there were three ships loading and 14 ships waiting, for a total tonnage of 645,000. As of June 1, the total tonnage in all ports was 1.2 million. In effect, over one month of grain transportation and hauling is required to fill the ships which are there at the present time. Approximately ten days earlier, there were about one million tons.
What is happening is contrary to the press release put out by the Liberal backbencher, and to what the minister has stated. We are slipping behind in our grain transportation. We are not catching up with the system at the present time. For example, the terminals at Thunder Bay approximately ten day ago were being used to a 40 per cent capacity. At the present time, the utilization is under 40 per cent and is continually dropping.
What are the effects? I have mentioned three before. One can understand why an investigation will be undertaken by someone in western Canada into the entire question of the movement of grain in Canada. We are faced with a somewhat difficult situation. China has bought grain from the United States at new high prices, in the neighbourhood of $4.55 per bushel. Canada is locked into contracts until the end of this crop year. Canada's contracts are over $1 per bushel less than the price being paid by China. The effects of the grain backlog will be a loss of shipment from country elevators.
The Canadian Wheat Board has commenced to revise downward the various quotas it expected to fill. Barley is an example. On the weekend I believe it was revised downward from 15 bushels to 12 bushels. That is an indication of the situation in which we find ourselves. The Canadian Wheat Board had counted on moving over one billion bushels from country elevators. At the present time the board has indicated that this will not happen. Also we are looking at demurrage charges caused by the waiting of ships which the farmers have to pay. The demurrage charges will amount to between $17 million and $20 million, which is the highest on record.
Some months ago the minister indicated that a record would be broken in the area of total exports. The Canadian Wheat Board indicated that the exports will amount to approximately 800 million bushels, which certainly will not break any record.
June 5, 1978

Substantial demurrage is being paid at both west coast and St. Lawrence ports for the first time in our history.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext: That is not true.

I would like to indicate to the Minister of Transport that the Canadian Wheat Board indicated this is the first time it has happened. Furthermore, the total carryover will be much larger than anticipated.
All hon. members would urge the government to act on the Canadian Wheat Board request for some 4,000 additional hopper cars, and funds for refurnishing an extra 5,000 boxcars. One important factor which we tend to overlook, and to which the government has not addressed itself, is car turnaround time. In other words, I am referring to the amount of time necessary to ship a car of grain to one of our coastal ports, unload it, and return it to western Canada. According to the grain trade, the length of time required is approximately 20 days. That has not dropped significantly over the last 15 to 20 years.
The situation regarding grain export is so bad at the present time that an official of the Alberta Wheat Pool in Vancouver stated that the wheat pool is forced to write off Friday as a work day, because railways run out of cars on Thursday. The cars are available once again on Saturday, but the pools are forced to pay workers double time to load them on weekends.
In his speech before the Vancouver Board of Trade, the Minister of Transport stated that bad weather, late arriving ships, and the temporary loss of a rail bridge have delayed deliveries. He said, "We are only now inching back". According to the Canadian Wheat Board, that is not true. Also he said the following:
We are looking this year at exporting 850 million bushels, which means a total delivery by the producers of one billion bushels.
Also that statement is not true. This statement was quoted in the Canadian Press on June 1, just a few days ago. In fact, it was on the same day when the startling figures regarding the amount of tonnage waiting in our various ports were made public.
How bad are the rail lines in western Canada? The rail system in the west has been neglected for such a long time that great sums of money will be needed to rehabilitate many lines. Certainly that statement does not have to be made in western Canada because everyone is aware of it. The Hall commission reported that branch line subsidies have not gone back to the branch lines. These subsidies have gone to the railways. In turn, the railways have taken this money and used it where they saw fit. Over the years the system has been neglected. We are paying the price of close to $20 million in demurrage this coming year. Also there are the international problems we are having with our customers. Carl Snavely, the Washington economist who conducted the studies on the cost of transporting grain by rail, indicated that the current state of branch lines is fairly bad. Also he suspected that without major repairs the system could start to break down within a very few years. Of course that is happening at the present time.
Grain
Mr. Jim McDonough who was the executive director of the Hall commission before going to the Canadian Transport Commission, has echoed the same concerns. When the Commission started its hearings, he reported that railway officials were asked to estimate the life expectancy of prairie rail lines. Those officials indicated that if no significant maintenance work was done the life expectancy of various lines would vary from one year to 15 years. That possibility is rearing its ugly head at the present time.
The report of the Hall commission is a central issue to this motion. The government announced that it was going to look into the entire question of western rail lines in April, 1975. Mr. Hall tabled his report on May 19, 1977. Thus, it has been well over a year since the results of the study were made known. Mr. Justice Hall made approximately 92 recommendations. Six of those recommendations have been implemented, three have been partially implemented, 25 apparently required further study, and 58 have not been commented upon at all.
It would be interesting to have a look at some of the recommendations brought out by the Hall Commission and compare them to the responses given by the government. We should be provided with an opportunity to view both the recommendations of the commission and the responses of the government in as impartial a light as possible.
The first recommendation of the Hall commission was the establishment of a prairie rail authority. The government has established the Prairie Rail Action Committee.
The second recommendation was in the area of compensating the railways for the cost of moving grain. The Hall commission recommended the actual cost of moving grain minus the Crow rate level. The government's response was that it would cost $200 million, which was too expensive, and it could not afford to do this at the present time.
Another recommendation had regard to the fact that it would cost some $35 million annually, including inflation, to close the discriminatory gap between raw and finished products. The minister's response to that was that he thinks the figures are wrong and does not believe them.
The commission recommended the establishment of a northern development railways department of the CNR. The minister has indicated he will review that.
The Hall commission recommended that we eliminate the railway stop-off charge for in transit grain, to which the government has said no.
The commission recommended the utilization of the Canadian government elevator at Saskatoon for cleaning, storage and shipment of grain to Churchill, to which the government has said no.
The Hall commission recommended the construction of a government elevator at Yorkton. There has been no construction started, so that represents the government's reply. In that regard perhaps the House would be interested in hearing a

June 5, 1978
Grain
paragraph from the Western Producer report of April 20, 1978, where it is stated:
The report on the feasibility of the port of Churchill and the proposed terminal at Yorkton was solicited by the federal government after the Hall report was published.
Mr. Hall's report recommended that stop-off charges at inland terminals be eliminated so grain can be cleaned and reshipped from inland terminal points. He recommended a 25 to 30 million bushel terminal be built at Yorkton to provide surge capacity for the port of Churchill and the insurance rates be readjusted to allow for a longer shipping time.
With these and other recommendations the port of Churchill could realistically handle 55.5 million bushels, Mr. Hall says. Last year 30 million bushels were shipped from the Hudson Bay port.
The Bryden report-
That is the report that really cancelled the recommendation of Mr. Justice Hall. It states:
The Bryden report didn't share Mr. Hall's optimism for the Churchill facility.
The article goes on to state:
"From beginning to end it is loaded against not only the facility at Yorkton but also the feasiblity of the port of Churchill as an ongoing force in western Canada-"
The report concludes by stating:
"We have a report downgrading the Hudson Bay Route, downgrading the port of Churchill and negative to a grain handling facility at Yorkton. I might say this is a serious problem" Mr. Hall told the 75 Bay supporters.
Mr. Hall said it was strange that no one from the port of Churchill, the manager of the port of Churchill or the federal port authority was interviewed when the Bryden report was tabulated.
He goes on to be very critical of the government for its handling of what he considers to be certainly one of the commission's more central recommendations. That is the kind of stonewalling tactic that we have seen on this side of the House, and that Mr. Justice Hall has experienced.
As the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) has indicated, the government has to make a commitment to this report in its totality.
Another recommendation of the commission was to enlarge and modernize the terminal at Prince Rupert to a capacity of some 6 million bushels. The government has started in this regard and has allocated some money, but at the present time it is waiting to see whether or not the grain companies will utilize that facility.
Mr. Hall also recommended that we eliminate the additional charge by the railways of 14 cents per 100 pounds levied on rapeseed meal on hopper cars. The government's response to that was no.
The commission recommended that abandoned rights-of-way be returned to provincial Crown. The response to that was that it will go back to the federal authority and then to the municipalities.
The commission recommended the establishment of a Canadian Wheat Board regional liason office in Alberta and Saskatchewan, but certainly up to the present time the answer has been no.
There are many other areas and recommendations in the Hall commission report that have not been implemented. Mr. 
Justice Hall recommended that the Canadian Wheat Board should provide information to producers on rail car allocation to specified stations and blocks upon request, but to my knowledge that has not been implemented.
The commission recommended the establishment of an offline elevator at the Fisher Branch, Manitoba. Of course, that has not been done.

speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh A. Anderson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may seem odd to some hon. members that a member of parliament from British Columbia should be involved in a debate basically dealing with the movement of grain in western Canada. Hon. members should recognize the fact that British Columbia, through the port of Vancouver and the port of Prince Rupert, plays a very important role in the movement of grain to our customers around the world.
There is no question but that the port of Vancouver has on occasion received odd knocks from people regarding the shipment of grain out of that port, but the facts indicate that the port of Vancouver is developing into the largest exporting port on North America's west coast. Vancouver leads every other port on the western seaboard, with 47 million tons being handled in 1977. Canadian Press reports indicate that port general manager, Fred Spoke, claims he can see the day when Vancouver will equal all the west coast ports combined.
It should be remembered that grain handlers are making major improvements in their handling capacity, and railways are also busy with substantial improvements to their west coast efforts. According to Mr. Spoke, Burrard Inlet, a major grain outlet, can handle ships up to 120,000 deadweight tons which, he notes, is something that almost no other harbour in North America can boast. In short, the port of Vancouver is doing its job well, and is gearing up to do even better in the future.
It has been estimated that in the calendar year 1978 shipments of grain out of the west coast will total approximately 300 million bushels. I understand the minister's target for the west coast in the early 1980s with the Prince Rupert and Vancouver facilities enlarged, is in the neighbourhood of 450 million bushels.
It may be that many residents of the province of British Columbia are not aware of the significance of the grain trade through our two major ports, or what this means to the economy of British Columbia. 1 do not have the figures before me, but I can assure hon. members of this House, as well as British Columbia, that with the expansion of port facilities, the trans-shipment of grain through the two ports will contribute more and more to the economy of British Columbia in future years.
In his remarks the minister stated that by the year 1982 over one billion bushels of grain will be shipped out of the
June 5, 1978

Lakehead through Thunder Bay, Vancouver and Prince Rupert. At the present time there is an imbalance in the amount of grain shipped out of Thunder Bay compared to the ports of Vancouver and Prince Rupert. I understand that by 1982 the two areas of shipment will be almost equal with approximately 500 million bushels to be shipped out of British Columbia and approximately 500 million bushels to be shipped out of Thunder Bay.
There are plans for expansion of grain storage facilities in British Columbia. Hon. members will be aware that not too long ago an elevator burned down and destroyed part of our capacity for shipping out of the port of Vancouver. I understand the Alberta Wheat Pool is planning to expand storage facilities by 2.8 million bushels, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool is planning an expansion of 3 million bushels of storage, the United Grain Growers is planning an expansion of 2 million bushels and the Pioneer Grain Company an expansion of 2.6 million bushels. In the next few years we can foresee an additional 10.4 million bushels of storage capacity added to the existing 23 million bushels storage facilities in the port of Vancouver. At the present time we have 2.25 million bushels storage capacity which would give us a total of approximately 35 million bushels of storage capacity in Prince Rupert and the port of Vancouver. Storage in Prince Rupert will be increased also and I will touch on that later.
It seems to me that the government's position on the statutory grain rate issue is crystal clear. The railways are ordinarily expected to make the major move with regard to the provision of adequate capacity as movements are projected and foreseen. I think it would be fair to say that up to this time the railways have been doing a competent job. To assist them and to assure that they would do the job, in each of the last two budgets there have been significant changes and improvements in the capital cost allowance for the railways so that their cash flow may be improved. It would also be fair to say that they responded with plans to expand their capacity more rapidly where they foresaw increased freight.
The big exception in the railways' capability to do what is needed for freight has been in the area of grain. As the Snavely commission pointed out, the railways receive very little for grain movement compared to the cost of moving it. The Hall commission stated that there is a call upon government to do additional things in the way of financing, to ensure that the railways have the funds, notwithstanding the continued existence of the long standing statutory Crow rate on grain.
It is no secret, Mr. Speaker, that in this House on many occasions I have criticized the CPR, especially in British Columbia and on Vancouver Island, for their insensitivity to the travelling public in asking for cessation of passenger service. We have the situation in western Canada, however, that with the statutory Crow rate, funds are not generated to enable the railroads to maintain their road beds and to retire and purchase rolling stock in order that we can make the continued expansion of exports which, as I indicated earlier, it had been estimated by the year 1982 would reach one billion
Grain
bushels shipped out of Canadian ports. The money has to come from somewhere, Mr. Speaker.
The government foresaw the Hall commission's recommendation regarding financing for the railways. In our 1975 policy statement we made clear that, where it is a matter of policy to maintain rates at a level below cost, the government should be willing to identify that policy and its cost and pay the amount of money to the transportation system expected to bear the burden. Therefore, it would not have to pass the costs of that transportation system on to other people or, indeed, need it be inadequately provided for.
The government responded to the spirit of that requirement for an additional infusion of cash with the provision of 8,000 hopper cars for the movement of grain, at a cost of $255 million. That was the first real, important move forward toward improving our grain handling system in some 40 years. The government also set up the Hall commission and the Snavely commission and have been dedicating themselves toward implementing their reports. In this moment of fiscal restraint we do not have the ability to move at once to pay to the railways what the Hall commission recommended, I think that point must be underlined: in this moment of fiscal restraint we do not have the ability to move at once to pay to the railways what the Hall commission recommended. There is no question that many of the recommendations are worthy of consideration. There are many other areas, however, that demand government attention.
If we had unlimited funds to enact the Hall commission's recommendations, we would still require additional funds for the enlargement of port facilities. It would be foolish to have one billion bushels of grain moved across the prairies through British Columbia only to find that the terminals could not handle one billion bushels of grain. I therefore believe that we have to look at the total transportation system and not just rely on certain sections of it. This is what I think the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has done by announcing funds to be allocated to the port of Vancouver and the port of Prince Rupert.
What the government and the minister did was immediate and of fundamental importance. The most important thing was to see that the railways went ahead with investment in grain lines on the prairies which had been neglected. Within a matter of a few weeks of the tabling of the Hall commission report, the government transferred to the basic rail network the additional 1,813 miles which the Hall commission identified for that purpose.
Likewise, the enormous additional expenditure required to extend the Crowsnest rates to processed grain products is beyond the capability of the federal government at this time. If this subsidy were extended to processed products, it would be very difficult to limit it just to the products that currently move by rail. Products presently moving by truck would quickly move by rail if this subsidy were not extended to truck movements of such products. It would also be argued that processed products in the east as well as those in the west should move under these rates; otherwise there would be a
6068

June 5, 1978
Grain
preferential rate which would not be accepted by other regions of the country. We would have to extend it to all modes of transportation and all regions of Canada, not limiting it to one carrier or one region.
If all such movements were included under the Crowsnest rate, the cost could conceivably be in excess of $200 million annually. This is in addition to the $200 million which would be required to compensate the railways for the full cost of moving the products currently covered by the Crowsnest rates. Day in and day out in this House we hear it argued that the government should spend wisely and be an example to provincial and municipal governments as well as to the individual. I suggest the additional funds required by the program I have just outlined would not be in the best interests of the country at this time. I am sure that further studies will have to be carried out to determine whether a policy of this type would ever be beneficial to the country.
I feel that the more you subsidize, the more you dislocate the natural patterns of transportation. One could get into an area where plants, whether they are manufacturing plants or otherwise, would be located in areas which would not normally be economically feasible for transportation reasons. As a result of subsidization further inequities are built in by locating plants and facilities in areas where they should never be located.
In his remarks the minister also included the embarkation by the federal government on a program to rehabilitate and upgrade the prairie rail network. I agree with this. The first phase is to cost $100 million and I understand will be completed by this summer. A second phase planned for 1979 and costing approximately $75 million has already been authorized by the Government of Canada. I would hope that the entire program costing over $700 million will be implemented during the expected eight to ten year period. I further hope that at the end of that period of time the basic rail network will be capable of handling hopper cars on a year-round basis.
I should mention a point that has been brought up in this House before, namely that we are in a record year of grain shipment at the Lakehead, the port of Churchill and also in the two B.C. ports. What has happened and what has not been recognized by some people is the fact that we experienced a very rough winter on the prairies. As a result of that we fell behind in the loading of ships at Vancouver and Prince Rupert and we are unable to catch up. There will always be problems in Canada with shipments of grain and other materials, for example potash, because of the climatic conditions. It does not matter what government is in power, climatic conditions will influence the transportation of goods and grain in this country. That is a fact of life that we have to look at.
We do not live or operate in a temperate climate, such as that in the southern United States. It is interesting to note that the port of New Orleans, which does not have the problems that we face in northern Canada, has approximately 30 ships waiting to load grain. And yet here we are in a record year in the shipping of grain, having had bad loading conditions

during part of our winter, and not being able to utilize hopper cars that traditionally switch over from the shipment of potash back to the grain trade, because fortunately or unfortunately the potash business is also having a record year. We have not had either the fast turnaround or the availability of cars which we have had in other years. This point should be stressed because variances in weather affect transportation in Canada. A second problem is the immense distances we must ship our goods. This sometimes is a blessing, at other times it is not. But obviously these things do play a role in transportation in Canada.
As I have stated, with the upgrading of the rail lines during that eight to ten year period of time and, with the expenditure of $700 million, we will have a first-class rail system. But again variances in weather will be a factor. These variances, of course, do not fall in the hands of politicians. After years and years of neglect and years and years of nothing being done with regard to the grain handling system, we have not only had in the last few years 8,000 hopper cars, but we have also had the commitment of the full amount of money required to put the basic rail network into first-class shape. That is an improvement and I congratulate the Minister of Transport, who is not the only Minister of Transport, Liberal, Conservative or otherwise, who has faced this problem. However, he is the minister, I believe, who has initiated a solution to this problem, and we are far along from what we were five, ten, 15 or 20 years ago.
The Hall commission recommended action with respect to Churchill and Prince Rupert. In both cases action has been taken and I am extremely pleased to see it, especially in the case of Prince Rupert. There will be advocates for Churchill among members from the prairie provinces, but in Prince Rupert the potential to move grain has always been there. However, for a variety of reasons that potential has never been achieved. Those of us who live in the southern part of British Columbia, which includes approximately 90 per cent of the population, have ignored areas such as Prince Rupert.
I am most pleased to see that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of Transport are redressing the balance which has always been in favour of Vancouver. It is a bold concept to have two major grain facilities in the province of British Columbia. I hope the day will come when Prince Rupert will play its proper role as a transshipment point for Canadian goods, not only grain. We are all aware that Prince Rupert is closer to the Asiatic markets than is Vancouver. I hope that those people who make decisions as to where goods are shipped from will recognize the importance of Prince Rupert-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of things that could be said in a debate of this sort. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) has outlined in his motion some seven or eight specific items and I would like to cover two or three areas which I
June 5, 1978

think are important. One is the question of rail line abandonment as it pertains to my riding and to some of the Hall commission's recommendations. Another point is the whole area of grain movement.
One of the things the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board failed to discuss was the whole question of government elevators in Canada and why those elevators are not being used to full capacity. We have five grain elevators owned by the Government of Canada, or inland terminals. Which are not being used to full capacity. If we were to use them to full capacity to dry the wet, the tough and the damp grain that is now being dried on the west coast, I maintain that we could be shipping much more grain and would be able to meet our commitments. As a result we would not be keeping ships waiting and paying demurrage fees.
Specifically, in this country we have five government elevators. There is one in Saskatoon with a capacity of some five and a half million bushels of grain. At the moment, according to our check, there is some 1,820,000 bushels of grain in that elevator. In Moose Jaw the capacity of that elevator is 5.5 million bushels of grain with some 955,000 bushels of grain presently stored there. In Calgary with an elevator capacity of some 2.5 million bushels some 625,000 bushels of grain are presently stored there. In Edmonton with an elevator capacity of some 2,350,000 bushels, only 378,000 bushels are in store. Lethbridge has an elevator with a capacity of 1,250,000 bushels but in store it has only 164,000 bushels. These five terminals owned by the Government of Canada, with a capacity of 17,100,000 bushels, at the moment have in store some 3,942,000 bushels.
I would like to ask, and perhaps the minister or someone else can reply later in the debate, why we are not utilizing more fully and efficiently government elevators on the prairies. Most of that tough and damp wheat that is now being cleaned and dried on the west coast comes from northern Saskatchewan and northern Alberta. If it does, why? Why do we not do as Hall recommends and drop these stop-off charges, and try and store some of that wheat on the prairies?
We have a capacity of 17 million bushels in those five government elevators. We could at least put 12 million bushels in them, but we now have slightly under four million bushels stored there. That means we are under-utilizing those facilities to a large degree. We have only about one third of the amount of grain in those elevators that we could have. That demonstrates a lack of leadership, a lack of efficient planning and a lack of seriousness in trying to move grain in this country on the part of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang).
There is something else I find rather strange, and the minister did not refer to this in his speech. The railways are not doing as well as they should be, particularly the Canadian Pacific Railway. I have before me the list of boxcars that have been hauled by the CPR and the CNR since the beginning of the current crop year until the end of May. As we all know, the CPR lines cover the area of the prairies where the majority
Grain
of the grain is grown, hauled and marketed. Despite that, so far this crop year CP has hauled less grain than the CNR.
The CNR has delivered to the west coast, Vancouver and Prince Rupert together, 58,322 boxcars. CPR, which has the obligation to haul more because it services more communities with more grain, hauled to the west coast some 49,287 carloads of grain. That is not good enough. The Minister of Transport should use his influence and power to ensure that the CPR hauls more grain to the west coast.
I look at December, which is probably the best month to get a comparison, to show where the CPR is falling down on the job. In December, CP hauled 2,750 carloads while CN hauled 4,284. I say to the Minister of Transport that I believe there is a lot more he could be doing. He could use his influence with CP. In fact, he could use his influence with both railways to make sure they are repairing and purchasing more cars, that they are hauling in a more efficient way grain to the west coast. Those government terminals could be utilized to a larger degree. He should ensure that grain being dried on the prairies and stored on the prairies could be moved to an export position when the rush and the bottleneck is not as great as at this moment.
The second matter I want to refer to in my all too brief 20 minutes this afternoon and this evening is another aspect of the Hall commission report that we should be talking about more than we do. That is the whole area of rail line abandonment as it pertains to ordinary communities in this country. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) mentioned that Hall recommended the establishment of a prairie rail authority to make a decision on over 2,000 miles of rail line on which Hall could not make a decision. He wanted more time to study the available data. He suggested that the PRA be established to look at these facts and make the decision as to whether these lines should stay or go.
I want to make a case for three lines that lie within the boundaries of my constituency. They are absolutely vital, not just to the people but to the communities and everything that one would call a community in about ten, 20 or 25 towns in my constituency.
The first line goes from Thunderhill Junction in Manitoba, which is near the town of Swan River, right on through Kelvington in central Saskatchewan. Mr. Hall recommended that that line be placed under the PRA. The line is 113.6 miles in length. It has 12 delivery points, namely Kenville, Durban, Benito in Manitoba, Arran, Pelly, Norquay, Hyas, Stenen, Sturgis in the eastern part of Saskatchewan, the division of that line, and also Preeceville, Lintlaw, Nut Mountain and Kelvington on the western portion of that line in Saskatchewan. The ten year average of hauling grain has been some 8.3 million bushels per year, or an average haul of some 73,000 bushels per mile.
For some reason, the Hall commission divided that line into two parts. They took the eastern part, from Thunderhill Junction near Swan River to Sturgis, and recommended that it be placed under the basic rail authority. The minister agreed and put it there when the Hall commission report came down a

while ago. The rest of the line, from the town of Sturgis out west, which is Preeceville, Lintlaw, Nut Mountain and Kelv-ington, was to be put under the auspices of the prairie rail authority.
As I said earlier, that does not make much sense. They are big communities, particularly Kelvington and Preeceville. They are centres for a whole series of farms and villages. They have good business sections and well over 1,000 people each. They are well established, progressive communities. They haul a lot of grain. It was a surprise to me, and I suspect from what he said privately to the minister himself, that that part of the line was not put under the basic network. The minister should take action at this time and place that line under the basic network and make sure that it is protected.
After the news came out, those communities decided to set up "save our rail line" committees. I was present at three public meetings in those communities, and at one meeting of the steering committee since then, to discuss ways and means of saving that rail line. I want to say as strongly as I can that it must be saved, not just for the farmers who haul their grain- although it is obvious that it must be saved for them because of cost and convenience-but for the business community and everyone who lives in those towns. If it is not, the towns will gradually dwindle in size and eventually disappear. While the whole thing is uncertain, it will be very difficult to persuade a new business to open or an existing business to expand because of the fear that the rail line will disappear.
As I said, under the leadership of some of the people in the areas, "save our rail line" committees have been set up and are working. The Minister of Transport should be in communication with those communities. May I call it six o'clock?

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was presenting an argument to the effect that the minister should move to retain the Preeceville-Kelvington rail line in the northern part of my Saskatchewan constituency. I made that argument on behalf of the farmers and townspeople there and I would point out that they have established a save-our-rail-line committee under the chairmanship of George Derbyshire of Kelvington and the secretaryship of Nora Vansdal of Lintlaw.
The second line about which there is uncertainty in my constituency is the line which runs from Canora to MacNutt. Under the Hall report this Canora-MacNutt line is divided into two regions; there is the MacNutt-Wroxton portion which is 15.7 miles in length. There are three delivery points in that

area, namely, MacNutt, Calder and Wroxton, and over the last ten years they have averaged some 1.7 million bushels of grain, which works out to about 105,000 bushels of grain per mile of track. The northern portion of that line runs from Ross Junction, which is right next to Canora, to the village of Wroxton and includes the delivery points of Hampton, Ryan and Stornoway.
There are ten elevators serving four different companies along that particular part of the line. It covers some 37.8 miles and over the last ten years the average amount of grain which moved over that line was 1.6 million bushels, or 42,000 bushels per mile. Once again, as in the case of the line, this line would serve six delivery points, and it is of keen interest to the people there that these rail communities are going to suffer and that the farmers will be spending a lot more money in transportation of their grain. Also, the towns and villages along the line will dwindle and so on. As in the case of the other line to which I have referred, the local people have also set up a save-our-line committee. It has been a very active committee; I have had a chance only to meet with them once at a meeting and once at the executive level. They are making progress, I think, in their fight to save the rail line. That committee is under the able chairmanship of Albert Zelaney of Wroxton and the secretary is Clarence Laidlaw of the town of Calder.
The third line in my area is a line which is slightly different from the first two. It was recommended by the Hall Commission that the first two go under the prairie rail authority. With a good fight I think there is good reason to be optimistic that they will be placed under the basic network, particularly if the Minister of Transport will listen with a positive attitude. I have always said there will be a tougher battle for the third line. It is the line that goes from the city of Yorkton to the little town of Willowbrook and to another little town called Jedburgh. That line includes some 26 miles of track. Over the last ten years an average of 900,000 bushels of grain per year have gone over that 26 miles of track, or about 34,000 bushels per mile. That line serves two very important communities in my riding which will be hurt if the rail line is abandoned, as it will be prior to 1981 unless something can be done to stop it. As in the other two areas a rail line committee has been established under the chairmanship of the reeve of that municipality, Mr. August Fenske, and the secretary of the rural municipality is also the secretary of the committee, Mr. Jerry Kuziak. Both of these men are from the Jedburgh-Theodore area.
I have before me a copy of an article which appeared very recently in the Yorkton newspaper This Week. The headline is: "Jedburgh starts fight to keep last elevator". I point this out because I think this is a new angle to use to help keep rail lines. The article says:
Last fall, the residents of Jedburgh and area formed a committee to organize a fight to keep their rail line to Yorkton, which under the Hall Commission recommendations could be abandoned in 1981.
But now the community and surrounding farmers find that even if they save the line, it might not be any good to them.
June 5, 1978

Three weeks ago, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool informed the local Pool committee and members that its elevator will close down at the end of the crop year, July 31.
With the United Grain Growers (UGG) elevator already closed, and being torn down this winter, that would leave the community without a delivery point for grain.
Save the Rail Committee chairman August Fenske told Yorkton This Week Saturday that the group has switched the emphasis of its efforts: right now it is working to keep the pool elevator open.
With the support of the local pool committee, the group has circulated petitions in the community and district demanding that the Pool keep its elevators open, and a meeting will be held this week to gather together the petitions and discuss the next course of action.
Wherever the petitions have been taken, they have received strong support, Fenske said.
"We'll either force them or convince them to keep it open," he added.
Here is a community which has to fight with the wheat pool itself to keep its elevator open. I encourage that community in that fight because back in 1974 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) promised that as long as there are elevators on a line, that line will not be abandoned. The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board also said something very similar back in 1974, and I want to put on the record one of his comments. He said, and I quote:
As long as the Liberal party forms the government and as long as producers wish to continue to deliver to the elevator of their choice, not one rail line will be abandoned.
That was the Minister of Transport speaking on June 11, 1974. If people in Jedburgh and in other communities get commitments from their elevators that those elevators will stay, then I want to make sure that the minister will remain true to the commitment he made. If the elevators stay, the lines should stay. If that happens, people will have their elevators and their lines to pull their communities closer together in the years to come.
I would like to make one other point about complaints we have been receiving in the last few weeks from the local level about the unorganized way of delivering grain to ships on the west coast, Thunder Bay or at the port of Churchill. This lack of organization affects many farmers in my area. Just today we completed a survey of some elevators in my constituency. A lot of grain is produced in the Melville area, and the Melville pool elevator is plugged. It cannot take any more wheat, and 25 per cent of the farmers in the area will not get their seed quotas in. Car orders this week are for numbers two or three wheat, oats and barley. Most of the other elevators, as well as Melville's, on this block are also plugged or will not get the seed quota hauling completed. I suggest that the time has come for the Minister of Transport himself to intervene to make sure that the seed quota is extended and that boxcars are available so that farmers can haul their grain and can get money to pay for their seeding expenses. The Carberry block is also in my area. It now overlaps with the part of my riding which goes into the riding of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). He is also having similar problems.
The Langenburg elevator is plugged, and 50 per cent of the farmers in the Langenburg area will not get their seed quotas

in. Much of the same is happening in the Bredenbury block. The Wishart elevator toward the western fringes of my riding is plugged, and a substantial number of farmers in that area also will not get their seed quotas in. I think the minister should be making sure that the seed quotas are extended beyond the June termination date so that these farmers can deliver their grain. The minister should be saying to the railways that they have an obligation to provide boxcars so that farmers can deliver their grain and can have income to meet their spring seeding expenses.

Farmers in my riding and in every other riding across the country cannot deliver their grain. Mr. Speaker, in the short time which is available in this debate I am not going to talk about the difficulties and the opportunities this Hall commission report gives to the government to get our rail systems working. Hon. members who have already spoken have made clear the difficulties farmers are now facing, particularly in the eastern half of the prairies. Farmers have a very violent type of feeling because all winter long they have been told how much grain the minister has been sending out of the country, but they know it is not going out of their districts because there is nothing moving to any great extent yet to the east.
I want to comment on the larger aspects of this problem. I see that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) is back in his seat. Today we in western Canada received a news release from the hon. member which says:
Assiniboia M.P. Ralph Goodale says the Government of Canada will initiate a special, immediate investigation into the efficient use of prairie grain handling and transportation facilities.
The very moment this press release was going all over the prairies telling people the government would investigate the grain handling system, the minister was here in this House telling us how well the grain system is working. Either the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and the hon. member for Assiniboia have their wires crossed or the hon. member issued this statement without the permission of the government; but if the hon. member is correct and this is the view of the government, it proves the very basis for this motion of no confidence moved by the New Democratic Party. The NDP has moved this motion expressing no confidence in the government. I will quote from the opening part as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government has failed to expand Canada's capacity to move grain to export position thereby jeopardizing the

Grain
Canadian Wheat Board's ability to compete successfully for expanding grain sales-
My comment on that is very blunt and to the point: where was the NDP this last ten years when this government systematically has been following a policy of trying to get rid of farmers on the ground that there were too many farmers and too much production? The NDP has supported this government and kept it in power for most of the last 15 years. Every time there has been a minority government the NDP has kept the Liberal party in power. It was the NDP which put the government into a minority position in 1963. Now the NDP at long last recognizes that its allies which it has been supporting all these years have not done the job they were supposed to do.
I want to quote into the record what the minister himself has said. A year ago when the commission's report came down, all members of parliament and, I suppose, all members of the news media received a report from the minister's office called "The Hall Report: An Inviting challenge for Prompt Action", a commentary by the Minister of Transport dated May 27, 1977. In it he uses the following phrases: "we will establish in western Canada a modern, top quality handling and transportation system for prairie grain". Boy, was that definite action! Another phrase reads: "we have had two years of study-we know the problems. Now we must move with solutions".
Where was the hon. member for Assiniboia yesterday and today when this press statement was issued? Has he heard about the solutions? The minister has gone up and down the prairies and has repeated in the House ad infinitum that they are building box cars, that they are rebuilding rail lines, they have done this, that and everything. But why, then, is there a tie up?
I know the reasons. One is that ten years ago the government decided, and has let the railways and the grain companies know, that we should get rid of a large number of grain farmers in western Canada and reduce the acreage by half. Program after program has been brought in, such as the program on supply management, the LIFT program, and the stabilization of income program which was brought in seven or eight years ago. All those programs which were brought in in 1970-1971 were designed to get rid of farmers and to reduce acreage by half. Now, it became clear in 1968 and 1969 that the world's grain markets were going up at a tremendous rate; this dawned on the minister only recently, so now he admits his policies have been wrong for ten years. That is why the government has failed. Why the NDP, which used to have an interest in farm problems, took so long to realize that this mess was occurring, I do not know, but I will come back to them in a moment.
Better late than never.

They have called for some parts of this program. Paragraph (f) was referred to by the mover of the motion. It reads:

To strengthen the principles of orderly marketing by returning the marketing of feed grains to the sole jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board and to include as well the marketing of flax, rye and rapeseed under the said board.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

The provincial governments in the west put this before the farmers in the form of a referendum. What did the farmers say? They said that they did not want it. The farmers believe in the Canadian Wheat Board, but they want some part of their produce available through the alternative marketing system, and this the NDP has failed to recognize. They have failed to recognize that one cannot take the words of wisdom from the leaders of the grain companies. Whatever the grain companies' leaders say, that is what the NDP says. And who tells the grain companies what to think? The Minister of Transport in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board does. He has these boys in his pocket.
When I see the NDP going along with this, I am ashamed of them. They used to be a strong voice for agriculture. What are they now? Just the spokesmen of the grain companies. The Minister of Transport today nailed those grain companies when he said why he had not brought in the prairie rail authority. He said it was because it was not wanted by the head of the Alberta Wheat Pool and the head of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. Where are those two guys going to hide, because the great majority of farmers in Alberta and in Saskatchewan want the prairie rail authority? They look on it as the Magna Carta of the whole economics of western Canada. But he nailed their hides to the cross today when he said they did not want it. So he was glad they put in the Prairie Rail Action Committee which was designed to keep any action from occurring.
All we have heard from the minister so far is when one of his colleagues said that we must set up a committee to study the studies. We have been studying the railway problems in western Canada since the 1930's and every royal commission until now has reported that we should rationalize the railway operation. The last study was undertaken by Mr. Justice Emmett Hall. He said now is the time for action; let us set up a rail authority controlled by westerners in charge of running the railway system over its marginal 2,000 miles until it can be demonstrated that the lines can be run for a profit, at which time they should be turned back to the railways. But the minister did not want that. So we have the prairie grain companies and the minister saying they will set up a cover-up called the Prairie Rail Action Committee, which will set up hearings but whose primary and only purpose is to try to keep action from being taken.
Now I will come back to what I believe is the key question in this resolution. Why did the NDP put in paragraph (f)? It is a motherhood paragraph but the farmers do not want it, just the grain companies. Actually, it is quite simple why the farmers do not want it. If you are selling grain to your neighbour or to the local feed lot or feed mill, if it comes out of the Wheat Board under the present rules, you have to take the grain to the elevator and the person who buys it has to pay for
June 5, 1978

the handling charges, the freight charges, the drying and cleaning charges, and all the other charges. If he has to ship that grain down to Thunder Bay, he takes it out to feed his stock and he is stuck with the 40 cent charge for services he did not get.
Because of that the farmers want the right to be able to deliver their grain to their neighbour or to the feed lot nearby. Many farmers have organized into co-operatives to do just that. That is why a great majority of the farmers in the west turned down the idea that all grain should be put into the Wheat Board by being put into the elevators. Everyone knows that the Hall commission report gave a lift to the livestock farmers in western Canada because it stated that now is the time to give livestock producers a fair break under the Crows-nest Pass rates. However, the report did not state how it should be done.
The commission wanted to end the discrimination which exists against farmers who have to buy their grain from the elevators and pay 40 cents for services they did not get. It wanted parliament and the government to come up with a way of handling this. As a matter of fact, the Conservative party has considered the recommendations of the Hall commission and looked for various ways in which this particular recommendation of Chief Justice Hall could be put into effect, and we have come up with three or four ways. All I will say is that these proposals, I think, try to meet the farmers' needs and still give them the benefits of the Crowsnest rates if they are livestock producers.
The first proposal I call the Devine proposal because it was thought up and first mentioned by Professor Devine of the University of Saskatchewan. I know he has been around to see the farm leaders and the heads of the governments of each of the provinces and he has made his ideas known far and wide, so I think he deserves the right to call his proposal his own. One of the Devine proposals to get around all these difficulties and come up with a workable solution to the problem of giving equal treatment to livestock producers and grain producers is that farmers haul their feed grain to the elevator, pay a service fee for the weighing and ticketing and let the buyer get his ticket as well.
As a result of this service, the seller of the grain gets the initial payment according to the daily reported price set by the Canadian Wheat Board, and in return for selling his grain through the system he becomes eligible not only for the initial payment of grain as set by the Canadian Wheat Board but also for the final payment, if there is one. On the other hand, when the grain has gone into the elevator and out, the buyer gets it at the going price of the day set by the Canadian Wheat Board, less the handling charges, less the storage charges, less the freight charges, less the cleaning and dockage charges and all the rest of it. Therefore, he gets the advantage of 40 cents a bushel, which puts him on a par with the eastern livestock feeder.
That proposal has both advantages and disadvantages, as do other proposals. I was interested in reading the other day about the government of Saskatchewan. At the present time
Grain
the government of Saskatchewan is NDP. The policy of the NDP was strongly stated a year ago, namely, that all grain should come under the Canadian Wheat Board. That is what the motion before us tonight calls for as well. After the vote by the farmers, who indicated that they did not want it in the first place, the Saskatchewan minister of agriculture had a change of policy. Now he is coming up with a new feed grain policy.
I should like to refer to The Rural Councillor of May 1, 1978. I hope hon. members of the New Democratic Party listen to what I am about to read. The Hon. Edgar Kaeding, the minister of agriculture for Saskatchewan, on March 15 said the following:
Under the proposal outlined by Mr. Kaeding, farmers would arrange farm to farm sales but such sales would be subject to quota restrictions and would be recorded in the sellers permit book. He would receive the initial payment and be eligible for any final payment that might be made. The elevator agent would weigh, grade, assess dockage and record the transaction on a fee-for-service basis. The purchaser would pay what Mr. Kaeding called a "revised corn competitive price for western Canada." This would be the lower of the Thunder Bay corn formula price or the Canadian Wheat Board asking price less the cost of getting the grain from Saskatchewan to Thunder Bay.
This is exactly the same system which I have just outlined called the Devine proposal. I gave credit to the author of the proposal. I am not stopping at Mr. Devine's proposal. The Conservative party is looking at several other proposals. I give credit for this proposal to the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers). He was the first member I heard talk about that, but other people have talked about it since. He comes from the province of Alberta, which is the biggest beef producer in Canada, producing approximately six million head of beef cattle. This is a simple system as well. The proceeds from the feed grain sales could be used to pay farmers the equivalent of the Crow rate in the form of a pro rata amount on the finished beef. In other words, the livestock producer would be given an amount equal to the cost of grain which went into raising the animals shipped for export under the Crowsnest rates. This could be done simply. It could be payments based on the differentials in various cities such as Edmonton, Calgary, Saskatoon, Regina, Winnipeg, or any other market centre. These would be added to the agricultural price support payments on a quarterly basis when they became due. This would provide a reward for finishing the animal in the west and would make the western feed grain user equal to the eastern feeder. It would mean an end to seeing our livestock industry moving out of western Canada.
That proposal contains good, simple points as well as bad ones. We cannot see ourselves as a Conservative government coming in here on the basis of the proposal of the hon. member for Red Deer or on the basis of the proposal by Professor Devine of Saskatoon and saying that this is the program. These programs are to remedy injustice and discrimination. Farmers should be consulted in a real way, rather than going ahead and consulting with the grain companies. One does not consult a weasel to learn how to run a hen house. One does not consult the grain companies alone concerning the interests of farmers. I do not care what grain companies call themselves.
