Grain
They can call themselves the Alberta Pool, the Saskatchewan Pool, UGG, Pioneer Grain or anything else. As far as farmers are concerned, they are the boys they have to get by.
Consultation does not mean only talking to one or two farm leaders and a grain company. There must be genuine consultation with the farmers. In that event agreements would be easier to reach. They would know that we are putting policy alternatives before them in order for them to express support or disagreement. Also they will know we have consulted them. This would take away the great anger and alienation on the part of farmers in western Canada. Some of these farmers feel that all the government does is meet with one or two of the grain companies and decide government policy on that basis. We would like to see genuine consultation.
With regard to the NDP motion before us, that party should be congratulated for realizing there has been a failure on the part of the government to provide infrastructure in order to move Canadian grain to market. The government is quite correct in saying that it cannot be stopped, and that the world will want at least one billion bushels long before 1982. In fact, the world wants that from us now, but it cannot be provided because the government sold all the 1976 and 1977 crops at $3 a bushel, which is below the current world price. With the current price of $4.50 at Vancouver, farmers are not very happy to see all their grain going out at low prices.
Therefore, our real job is to accept the Hall commission report. The guts of that report was the prairie rail authority. The prairie rail authority is a western board looking after western problems. For years the civil service took us through the hoops. The old transport board was in the hands of the railways. Then the Canadian Transport Commission was set up. That commission did not even wait to get out of the hands of the railways; it was there before the railways were. Now we have a bill to bring us back to the civil service again.
Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, today the House is considering a very important subject. I believe it is totally appropriate for parliament to devote this time to the question of the prairie grain handling and transportation system. The value of the prairie grain economy to the over-all national economy of Canada cannot be overemphasized. It is important to the west, indeed to all of Canada, to ensure a healthy and vibrant grains industry. Anything parliament can do through discussion of this kind to bolster the industry and to augment grain handling and our transportation capacity certainly is a worth-while undertaking.
Today I noticed a very interesting argument between hon. members of the New Democratic and Conservative parties concerning their respective positions regarding the strength of the Canadian Wheat Board. The position of the New Democratic Party probably is spelled out reasonably well in the motion before us. Members of the Conservative party take a different view. We have the publicly reported comments of the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), who suggested that the Canadian Wheat Board should be open to internation-

al competition. As well, the Conservative premier of Alberta launched a variety of attacks in recent weeks upon the Canadian Wheat Board.
For the benefit of hon. members opposite, and perhaps as a way for them to resolve this dispute among themselves, I should like to quote an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal dated June 3, 1978. It was written by a Saskatchewan journalist, Mr. Marc Lisac. He wrote a general commentary about the political scene in Saskatchewan. The article in part reads as follows:
Saskatchewan New Democrats tend to paint the minister as a Professor Moriarty of the grain trade. They fear for the future of the board under Lang.
At the same time, the board has been under attack recently by Premier Peter Lougheed. The Alberta government seems increasingly to view grain as a natural resource like any of the others now owned by the provinces. Lang has emerged as the federal agency's staunchest defender against Lougheed.
The conflict of opinion between the two opposition parties as expressed by Mr. Lisac is interesting. Perhaps he will assist opposition parties in sorting out their respective positions.
Our grain handling and transportation system is facing an enormous immediate challenge. Grain producers are concerned about it. They are concerned about keeping up with the ambitious shipping program of the Canadian Wheat Board for this season, and about keeping demurrage costs to the bare minimum. It is not uncommon for farmers to express worry about this kind of thing. Indeed, virtually every year when we get to about this point in the grain shipping season there is likely to be a good deal of concern about the allocation of quotas, the use of railway cars, the condition of branch lines, the cost of demurrage, and so on. For decades we westerners have grown rather accustomed to these sorts of worries, and to an almost constant flow of apparent bad news about our grain transportation system.
I suggest that in this year, 1978, the story is in fact fundamentally different. The immediate challenges are still there before us, but some basic initiatives are being advanced to cope with those challenges in an effective, long-term fashion. Major steps are now being taken to build toward a Canadian capacity to move one billion bushels of prairie grain to export markets each year.
If we must face a problem in the Canadian grains industry, the challenge of keeping up to our export opportunities is probably the best kind of problem. Surely the sort of situation we face this year, as troubling as it may be, is a far cry from the serious depression in grain incomes we had to face in the early 1970s when markets were tight, quotas were low and prices were painfully inadequate.
The fact that we are now facing a challenge in moving our grain fast enough means that market conditions are in fact good and that Canada occupies a strong position as a major world exporter. This has resulted from a number of factors over the last few years, including the market development programs of the federal government and of the Canadian
June 5, 1978

Wheat Board, the credit terms made available to foreign buyers by the federal treasury, key diplomatic and trade missions by Canada to major importing nations such as China and Russia, and federal encouragement for diversification into export sales of grains and oilseeds like barley and rapeseed, which were not major selling items for Canada before about 1970.
Fundamentally, of course, there are two key elements in our strong marketing situation; first and foremost is the excellent quality of the grains and oilseeds produced so efficiently by Canadian farmers; and secondly, the superb, continuing work of the Canadian Wheat Board. The Wheat Board and its agents have obviously done an excellent job in winning sales contracts and, consequently, the board has had to develop a vigorous grain shipping schedule for this season, demanding that virtually each month we set a new all-time monthly record in terms of the grain volume moved.
When we hear news reports about our being behind in moving grain this year, it is useful to note that this really means behind the record breaking target levels being set by the board itself. In fact, we are a considerable distance ahead of most actual past performances, and even with the peculiar difficulties we have had to cope with this winter-heavy winter weather through the Rockies, a major derailment, a key bridge that was damaged in the Vancouver area, the severe February storms on the prairies, and so on-we are still likely to set a new annual record or near record by the end of this crop year.
Another factor to bear in mind is that since late last summer export prices have been consistently moving upward. At the moment the price for number one C.W. Red Spring wheat is well in excess of $4 per bushel. Naturally, when you shoot for an all-time volume record you are going to tax the transportation system to its absolute limits, and that is what has been happening this year. We expect to move nearly 850 million bushels of grain this year. That is about twice as much as would normally have been moved, say, 12 or 15 years ago, which means we are clearly within range of hitting the billion bushel mark in just a very few years from now.
In respect of the current situation this year, I think it is important to get our problems and our challenges in perspective. In this respect, Canada's largest and most vocal prairie grain handling firm has had quite a lot to say in recent weeks about the grain handling situation. I am referring specifically to the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, and for the record I would like to quote an important series of Saskatchewan Wheat Pool radio reports on this question. First of all, I would refer to the radio report published by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool for May 19. That radio report in part reads as follows:
There has been a great deal said about shipping delays in Canada's grain industry this year but little, if anything, has been said about similar problems in competing countries. The result has been an impression that only Canada is the laggard while competing countries snap up the business that should be coming to this country. What are the facts?
Reuters news agency reported that New Orleans, a major American grain outlet, had nine ships loading grain and 39 vessels backed up and waiting.
During the first week of May, the United States Department of Agriculture set up emergency service in conjunction with the Interstate Commerce Commission with a view to sorting out the problem of an extreme shortage of rail grain
Grain
cars. Apparently, the situation is a "mess". It should be remembered that U.S. grain is also moved down a less costly internal river system.
In Argentina, the last report was that grain carriers were experiencing a 15 to 20 day delay in seeking loads. Buenos Aires reported 27 boats were waiting at Rosario Roads and nine at Santa Fe. In Buenos Aires itself, nine vessels were waiting. Argentine sources said delays of up to 30 days could be expected for vessels loading up river and completing cargo in Buenos Aires.
In Australia, strikes have caused considerable congestion and shipping delays in grain shipments over the past month. Remember that Australian grain is grown near the coast of that country.
Recognizing that there have been some problems in Canada, in mid April the Canadian Grain Commission reported total exports of Canadian grain were up by 17.5 per cent above those of a year ago. Producer deliveries to primary elevators were up by 10 per cent over the same 37 week period of a year ago. The commission reported that as of April 12th, Canadian bread wheat exports were 35 per cent higher than last year, durum was up 45 per cent, rapeseed 7.5 per cent and rye exports were running 75 per cent ahead of last year's comparable figure. It should also be noted that Canada has increased her percentage of world wheat sales, mainly at the expense of the United States.
Quite naturally, we can't afford to take any comfort from or be complacent about grain shipping problems in Canada or the countries that we compete with. On the other hand, we need to keep things in perspective and not swallow the nonsensical impression that Canada is some sort of inefficient exception in the world of grain exports.
On May 24, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool in another radio report had this comment to make:
Despite the difficulties encountered in moving grain from the prairies to export position on the west coast during the winter months, the Canadian Wheat Board reports its west coast shipping program is running well ahead of last year.
Figures for the end of March, show 5.5 million tonnes shipped through the West Coast, as compared to 4.6 million tonnes at the same date in 1977. Total Canadian grain exports at the same date were 1.8 million tonnes ahead of last year, and the board says they will approach the all-time record set in 1972-73 by the end of the year.
Finally I would refer to the pool broadcast of May 26 of this year which reads in part as follows:
With all that has been said about the cost of demurrage payments in recent weeks, it may be helpful to examine just what demurrage has cost over the past 10 years.
An analysis of demurrage paid during the crop years from 1967-68 to 1976-77 shows the average cost of demurrage per bushel of wheat marketed was 0.54 cents per bushel. Even when calculated on the basis of cost per bushel of wheat exported, it was only 0.61 cents per bushel.
The highest demurrage charges recorded were in 1973-74. Even then, they were only 2.14 cents per bushel of wheat marketed. The lowest demurrage was in 1967-68, a minuscule 0.002 cents per bushel of wheat marketed.
A similar analysis of demurrage paid on barley over the same period shows average demurrage costs of 0.30 cents per bushel marketed, or 0.38 cents per bushel exported.
Demurrage must be recognized as one of the normal and necessary costs incurred in the international grain marketing business. At a 10-year average of 0.54 cents per bushel of wheat marketed, it certainly is not out of line. Talking about lump sums can be very misleading. The objective should be to pay the least demurrage possible but again, it has to be kept in perspective. Remember that no demurrage is paid when grain isn't being sold.
I would make one more reference to the comments of this very large important grain handling organization across a good part of western Canada, particularly the province of Saskatchewan. I refer to a recent edition of the Regina Leader-Post where the Canadian Press was reporting on the general grain handling situation across the west. A part of the article reads as follows:

E. K. Turner, president of Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, said no one is ever satisfied with the way things go, and it is always a source of concern to see ships waiting for grain.
'But invariably, when you book heavily, it doesn't take much to disrupt the program,' he said.
'We are running at volumes comparable with last year and are in a position where we can set export records this year before the end of July.'
'Given that, things haven't been going as badly as people have painted. It also indicates our capacity for export is greater than it has been in the past.'
Obviously, if we now have the capacity to transport nearly twice as much export grain as could be handled by the system in the early 1960's, the grains system must have been subjected to some pretty important improvements in recent years.
In this connection we can think of the 8,000 grain hopper cars, the port co-ordinators, the rail cost disclosure legislation, the reciprocal railway routing agreements, the Mants report on boxcar allocations, the new quota system, the block shipping system, the Snavely investigation of railway costs, the special boxcar repair program, all the good work being done to implement the Hall report, and so on. These are all federal initiatives to help upgrade the system, taken during this past decade or so.
More modifications are obviously required and several key federal efforts are already under way. For example, there is the prairie branch line rebuilding program which will invest something in the range of $700 million of federal money to upgrade the prairie grain network to top notch condition in the next five to seven years. There is a major storage expansion now moving toward completion in Vancouver to boost our capacity and our flexibility in that port by something in the range of 40 per cent. There are the multi-million dollar development plans now in place of Prince Rupert and Churchill.
We have heard recent demands, of course, for more grain hopper cars and another grain boxcar repair program. Those demands in themselves demonstrate the success of those two federal initiatives which have been undertaken in past years. The federal government has been considering those ideas for some time and I would expect a positive response to both suggestions.
All of these measures will help, particularly in terms of our long-term prospects. But for the period immediately ahead we have to be certain we are getting the very most out of the facilities we already have. Efficiency in grain transportation and handling is extremely important in maximizing sales and minimizing demurrage-and that means dollars in the pockets of farmers.
That is why I was pleased to see this past weekend that the Government of Canada is initiating a special, immediate shortterm investigation into the operations of the railways, the grain companies and the transportation section of the Canadian Wheat Board to ensure full co-operation among all agencies with grain moving responsibilities, and the most efficient possible use of all available equipment and facilities. We have got to get the very most out of the system we have now.
[Mr. Goodale.l
The investigation, to be undertaken by an independent analyst with proven experience and expertise in the railway industry, should have the active co-operation of the railways, the grain companies and the transportation section of the Canadian Wheat Board. The objective is to ensure that maximum advantage is taken of every Canadian grain selling opportunity and that demurrage costs are kept to the absolute minimum. Farmers on the prairies are concerned that we make the very most of every sales opportunity, and that we stay on target with the Wheat Board's delivery program to satisfy our customers and avoid demurrage. In addition to the long-term measures already initiated to build toward a billion bushel export target, we need immediate short-term measures too to assure that the existing rolling stock is being used to the best possible advantage and that we are getting the very most out of what we have now.
I applaud the efforts to add more hopper cars to our existing fleet of 8,000 of these ultra-modern, federally-financed grain cars. I also agree that another repair program to save additional boxcars for grain movement is a useful effort for the government to undertake.
These initiatives-along with the federal government's prairie rail rebuilding program, the storage expansion at Vancouver, the development plans for Prince Rupert and so on-will help enormously in meeting that billion bushel target that is just ahead of us. But for 1978, the rest of this crop year and the rest of this shipping season, we have to be sure that we are getting the very best out of the system that exists at the moment. That is why I believe a serious, independent and expeditious investigation of the current efficiency of the operations of the Wheat Board's transportation section, the railways and the grain companies can help to achieve the best shortterm results for producers. That is obviously a priority concern. I hope that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) will get this effort under way quickly so that we can begin to see some benefits in time for the rest of this crop year and the balance of the 1978 shipping season.
Undoubtedly we have some significant challenges ahead of us in the short term and the long term, Mr. Speaker. We also have every reason to believe we will be able to meet those challenges effectively to the advantage of the grains industry, to the advantage of the Canadian grain producer in particular, and ultimately to the advantage of the national economy.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in the debate on this motion. I feel it is a timely motion in that there is a great deal of concern in western Canada regarding the movement of grain, particularly in this season.
While the minister is still optimistic that grain exports will reach a record level, we are faced with the prospect of the inability to fulfil our export commitments on schedule. This, of course, could result in our customers losing faith in our delivery capabilities and looking elsewhere to fill their needs. In addition, we are faced with the possibility of demurrage charges estimated at between $17 and $20 million, possibly the
June 5, 1978

highest we have ever seen. As the law now stands, this $17 to $20 million will be charged to the Canadian Wheat Board and taken out of the producer pools. In other words, this money will come out of the pocket of the producer.
It has been suggested by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) that we should not talk about bulk figures but, rather, that we should be relating this $17 to $20 million to the number of bushels involved so that we would end up with a fraction of a cent per bushel in demurrage charges. Whether we talk about cents per bushel or the over-all total, it is still dollars and cents out of the pocket of the western grain producer. A buck is a buck, Mr. Speaker, no matter how you look at it. Added up, this is a substantial sum.
If you consider the multiplier effect on our economy, which is usually estimated at three times the initial amount, then if we hit a $17 to $20 million demurrage charge this year it means an over-all loss to the western economy of between $50 and $60 million, a very substantial amount. In fact, if you consider the cost of a hopper car at $40,000 and look at a loss of $60 million, this means that with that money we could purchase another 1500 hopper cars.
It has been suggested on the government side of the House that there is little we can do to cut down on demurrage charges. Mr. Speaker, boats do not suddenly appear in port without warning. They move relatively slowly. They have continuous radio contact with the shore and Canadian Wheat Board officials must know well in advance what ships will be arriving, when, and the grade and quantities of wheat required. If this information is known, I find it difficult to understand why the scheduling of grain movement cannot be carried out in such a manner that the types, grades and quantities of grain are available for loading when the ships arrive.
I believe that the Canadian Wheat Board has done an excellent job under very difficult circumstances. As has been pointed out by previous speakers, despite the fact that the taxpayers of Canada have supplied the railways with some 8,000 hopper cars since 1972, our capacity is now less than it was when we started purchasing hopper cars.
In addition-and this was mentioned by a previous speaker-as a result of questions asked in the transport committee it was determined that 23,000 CNR boxcars are presently in use in the United States on a no-charge basis. While I appreciate there is always an interchange of grain cars between Canada and the United States, these 23,000 boxcars are some 10,000 cars more than normal. If these 10,000 cars were presently operating in our system, we could have moved a tremendous amount of grain to export positions and we would not be faced with the possibility of very high demurrage charges which the Wheat Board is now anticipating.
I am sure that the hon. minister in charge of the Wheat Board must have been aware for some months of the problems at the west coast. As minister in charge of transport, he must have been aware of the boxcar situation. It would seem to me that he personally, or his senior officials, should have been
Grain
continuously monitoring the boxcar situation. They should have anticipated a problem and kept in touch with senior officials of both railways in an attempt to alleviate the problems we are now facing and have been facing for many months. Surely that is the responsibility of the minister, Mr. Speaker?
Over the past several years I have urged the further utilization of government inland terminals. I have asked questions and I have made recommendations without success. The five terminal elevators located at Moose Jaw, Saskatoon, Calgary, Edmonton and Lethbridge have a storage capacity of some 17 million bushels. On a two-shift daily operation they have a cleaning capacity of some 440,000 bushels per day. On a five-day week operation these plants, working on a three-shift basis, have an annual cleaning capacity of 114 million bushels, or a six-day capacity of 205.9 million bushels. It is interesting to note that the terminal elevator at Moose Jaw which has a capacity of 5.5 million bushels can handle in a year a throughput of between 25 and 30 million bushels. That same elevator in a 24-hour period, using unit or solid trains, is able to load sufficient cars to fill a one million bushel boat. Yet, we are not using these facilities.
Mr. Justice Hall and his commission did a study of inland terminals. He had this to say, and 1 will read from page 235 of the report:
The commission recommends the full use of the government elevators and the construction of another one at Yorkton.
The commission does not look upon the government elevators as replacement for any of the current terminal capacity facilities, but as an addition to systems capability of handling grain.
The commission recognizes that even with the elimination of the stop-off charges that there are going to be additional handling costs associated with the utilization of the government elevators. However, these should be more than offset by the ability to respond to market opportunities; to achieve such things as the elimination of demurrage of waiting ships, and the ability to use all the ports more effectively.
I am satisfied that the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) have little interest in the utilization of these facilities because to date they have taken no steps in that direction. Had they done so, we would have at least reduced the tremendous demurrage charges that the Canadian Wheat Board is now estimating. It must be remembered that these charges are incurred through no fault of producers. The producer has no control over them, yet he is expected to pay for them.
I concur with subparagraph (e) of the motion that is before us today which calls on the Canadian Wheat Board to be reimbursed by the treasury for the demurrage charges. As a matter of fact, on May 24 I put a question to the minister in the House. It is recorded in Hansard at page 5682. I asked the minister, without going into the preliminaries, the following:
Will the minister give an undertaking that all or a portion of the demurrage charges will be borne by the public treasury for this year?
The minister, with his usual skill, sidestepped the question and accused me of using imaginary figures when I quoted $17 million to $20 million. The figures I used, Mr. Speaker, were figures that came from the Canadian Wheat Board, the board

for which he is responsible as minister. He then went on to pat himself on the back and talked about the record movement of grain. He said this at page 5683 of Hansard:
We have a system that can handle twice as much as ever had to be handled during the regime of the right hon. gentleman for Prince Albert, because we are up to twice as much in our regular pattern.
A few minutes later the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton) stood up on a question of privilege to clarify the situation at page 5687 of Hansard. This is what he said:
In 1963, the last year of the Diefenbaker administration, when wheat was still king, we exported wheat and flour to the tune of 592 million bushels, an all time record, representing 28.4 per cent of the world market. In 1976-77, the record year under the present minister, it was down to 494 million bushels, 21 per cent. This year so far 350 million bushels have been exported-below 20 per cent of the world market.
That is an interesting fact when one considers that 1963 was the record year for wheat and flour exports, and that record has not been exceeded since that time.
People on the prairies are extremely disappointed, as are members of the opposition, that the minister has shown such reluctance to implement the provisions of the Hall commission report. We are disappointed as well that it was more than a year after the report was tabled that the minister first met with Mr. Justice Hall. He has been reluctant-and I am being kind when I use that word-to have Mr. Justice Hall appear before the transport committee. Had it not been for a renegade member of his party who voted with the opposition in committee, Mr. Justice Hall would never appear before the committee. Yet what did the hon. minister say in May 1977, 11 days after the Hall commission report was handed down? He said in his news release before he spoke at a meeting of various farm associations in Regina, and I quote:
With the unanimous urging of westerners for prompt, decisive responses to the Hall report, I am determined to act as expeditiously as possible to deal with the commission's proposals.
We will establish in western Canada a modern, top quality handling and transportation system for prairie grain. We have had two years of study-we know the problems. Now we must move with solutions. Now is the time for action. I look forward to your active participation and co-operation in the task ahead.
Almost in the next breath in the same speech he shoved aside one of the major recommendations of the Hall commission, a recommendation which the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) calls the backbone of the Hall commission report. That was the setting up of a Prairie Rail Action Committee. If one refers to the Hall report, one will find that the idea of the setting up of the authority was to study the rail lines that were in doubt. I quote from page 31 of the report:
This commission is not recommending the addition of another permanent branch to the already over-burdened bureaucratic tree. On the contrary, we believe that self-liquidation should be the ultimate goal of the Prairie Rail Authority, as will become apparent in what follows:
Time will not permit me to list the purposes of the organization, but the idea was that this prairie rail authority would monitor the lines that were in doubt, the lines that were being
(Mr. Neil.)
considered for abandonment. What happened? The minister set up what he calls the Prairie Rail Action Committee which is required to make decisions on rail lines by December 31 this year, decisions based primarily, I suspect, on some of the evidence which the Hall commission gleaned since the Prairie Rail Action Committee does not intend to hold any public hearings.
In my own area, I have a line, the Euston Junction-Colonsay line, made up of some 108.5 miles. This line carries annually over five million bushels of grain. Mr. Justice Hall and his committee made certain recommendations, one of which was to turn a portion of that line over to the prairie rail authority for consideration. The prairie rail authority, of course, would consider it over a period of three years.
What did the Prairie Rail Action Committee do? It arbitrarily decided against the recommendations of the Hall commission report and chopped off a substantial portion of the line that was to be studied. I will quote briefly from a letter I received from a gentleman in my district who, I believe, is secretary of an organization which is most concerned. He says this about the abandonment of that portion of the line from Liberty to Dilke:
The Prairie Rail Action Committee has given its recommendation without consulting anyone in this area and has done so in a very secretive manner. The pros and cons of abandonment are many and varied. We feel that the pros balance the cons and we need an explanation for the actions of the PRAC. This committee, we feel, is operating in a manner that can be described as approaching "total abandon".
That is the manner in which PRAC is operating. It will not listen to the people involved. In this instance, I understand that the elevator companies, the railways and the people in the districts were anxious that the line remain, yet the Prairie Rail Action Committee arbitrarily, without consultation, recommended the abandonment of a substantial portion of the line.
When I raised a question in the House, the minister suggested that the matter would be considered by the Canadian Transport Commission. A day or so ago I was at the transport committee meeting. Mr. Benson, chairman of the CTC, was in attendance. With regard to the lines which the PRAC is recommending for abandonment, he said his committee would not on its own take any action to hold hearings and it would only be on the basis of strong representations or recommendations from people in the various communities that they would hold hearings.
I see my time is up, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to participate briefly in this debate to deal with three narrow aspects with regard to the motion before us. The first aspect, which has not been dealt with in any specific way by the minister, is item (d) which calls on the government:
-to reimburse the Canadian Wheat Board for costs of demurrage charges on ships delayed in loading through no fault of the producers or grain companies;
I hope the House will pay careful attention to that provision. Coming from the Pacific coast, I have some sympathy for western grain farmers who are continually forced to pay demurrage. This year it is estimated it will probably be
June 5, 1978

between $17 million and $20 million. They are continually forced to pay demurrage through no fault of their own. The fault lies with the minister and his failure to pressure the railway companies to provide sufficient rolling stock to move the grain so that the 20 ships sitting in the harbour of Vancouver will not have to wait and wait while the farmer continues to pay and pay.
Inherent in that provision of the motion before us is that the minister be provided with some incentive to get to work and have the rail cars provided so that we can move our grain. It is not as though there are Canadians sitting idly by not wanting to build those rail cars. As the minister knows, there is in Squamish, B.C., a rail car plant that would be very anxious to get contracts to provide those kinds of railways cars.
What is the minister's basic response in terms of some incentive to get the railway companies to build those cars? Of course, there is the business of the 6 per cent. I quote from the Star Phoenix:
The latest government incentive to the railways came in the April 10 budget when it was announced that railways can claim another 6 per cent a year depreciation allowance on equipment purchased between now and 1983.
That is a typical Liberal government response, not tying the 6 per cent to the kinds of cars needed to move grain. The railway companies are not going to throw in a whole pile of money to support the Crow rate, which we on this side continue to support. They will buy oil cars to move oil and other cars where there is some profit. Where there is a low profit margin, they are not going to buy the hopper cars.
The minister has failed to use the muscle he should in terms of such things as the budget. That 6 per cent should have specified hopper cars. They should have specified the kind of rolling stock that is necessary to move grain out of the prairies to the Pacific in order that we can satisfy some of our customers.
Since 1972 I have sat in this House listening to this government blame the grain handlers' union for failing to move the grain, and blaming the bridge in New Westminster, which always seems to be out somehow so that they cannot move the grain. That bridge is very rarely out. It is not often that a ship hits that bridge. So that approach is ruled out. But excuse after excuse continues to come from the other side of the House for failure on the government's part to deal with problems which have been apparent for years. The grain handlers cannot be blamed this time. I want to quote Mr. Henry Kanes, head of the grainworkers union:
Canada will lose its foreign grain markets if the federal government doesn't smarten up and make sure the grain is delivered to waiting ships.
That is from a story in the Star-Phoenix. Mr. Dennis McDermott, president of the CLC, said the federal government should not have allowed the fleet of railway boxcars to deteriorate. Mr. Kanes further stated:
The Americans are going to pick up the Chinese trade and now the Japanese are complaining about delays in delivery.
Grain
That is the opinion of the head of the grainhandlers union. The grain handlers want a chance to co-operate with prairie grain growers to move the crop but the minister has not taken the aggressive action necessary. I think the grain handlers are now prepared to work around the clock. The trouble is they cannot put in three shifts in 24 hours if there are not enough cars to carry the grain from the prairies to the coast. The blame lies on the minister's refusal to put pressure on the railway companies to provide the cars which are needed. It is no good offering an incentive in a general way; the 6 per cent depreciation allowance does not apply specifically to the railway companies or to the boxcar shortage. It is interesting to note that a shortage of cars always occurs where there is a fixed statutory rate. As long as there is free enterprise and managed rates a need for intervention arises if an appropriate supply of boxcars is to be maintained.
The motion says that the government has failed to expand Canada's capacity to move grain to export positions. The operative word there is "capacity". In 1972 we had 26,000 rail cars for grain movement. Now, six years later, we have 13,000 cars and 8,000 hopper cars. So there is less capacity than in 1972. Responsibility for this situation lies with the minister: it is the result of his failure to understand that we must maintain and improve the carrying capacity in order to move grain quickly into position so as to satisfy Canada's customers.
The port of Vancouver is not taking the blame for this one. The workers there are ready to do their all to move the grain. The government has failed to give the necessary instructions, or, if you like, the incentives. We would like to get some jobs in British Columbia. We have a rail plant under-employed at Squamish while the country is chronically short of rail cars. It boggles the mind that the management of our affairs should be so poor. Why cannot we put those two factors together- unused capacity to build rail cars and a shortage of cars not only to move wheat but lumber, cattle, potatoes and other products. This minister cannot piously wring his hands and suggest that difficulties of one kind or another are always with us and that, after all, we are moving more grain than ever before. Mr. Speaker, wheat sells itself. The Wheat Board sells wheat.
Even the minister smiles at that!
The minister takes credit for what others have done. The world is starving for our wheat. The Canadian people know that credit for selling it does not belong to the minister.

They don't need the minister taking credit for every bushel the Chinese people decide to buy. We could lose our markets as a direct result of the government's failure to plan for the provision of rolling stock.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Milne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see that the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith) is trying to

June 5, 1978
Grain
catch your eye. I assure him my remarks will be brief and that he will have an opportunity to contribute to the debate before ten o'clock.
As I followed the discussion it seemed to me that most of the comments were related to the export of grain and wheat. Little was said about the importance of moving grain to eastern Canada where it is used in great quantities as feed for poultry and other livestock. I am pleased we have a minister who has done so much for the industry, particularly in connection with the transportation of grain. If the system had not been rationalized and if many difficult and expensive decisions had not been taken, much more of the market would have been supplied by grain from the United States. So we would not underestimate the importance of the efficient transport of grain from the west to eastern Canada.
I was introduced to the subject matter of this motion long before the hon. member tabled it. When I was a small boy, my father and cousin would go together in the winter time and buy a carload of grain. It was my job, along with my cousin, to bag the grain and we would team it back home. We have short memories but sometimes I remember those days not long ago, and the tremendous amount of labour involved in moving a relatively small amount of grain. I wish I could find time to go to the farm and look up some of the old waybills which are undoubtedly still there; in those days the loads were much smaller than they are today. When I am at the farm I sometimes see how the grain comes from the west now-the size of the cars and the ease with which their contents are unloaded and put through the milling process. I marvel at what has been achieved but I cannot help thinking back to the days when the work was all done by hand.
Earlier this year I had an opportunity to visit many farm communities in Saskatchewan while I was in western Canada.
I listened to the comments of people in many farm communities on the subject of the rebuilding of rail lines and the movement of grain. I was much impressed by what I heard. There is no doubt that when we are thinking in terms of the best possible use of money available to the government a commitment to the western grain system of $600 million or $700 million is a very large one indeed.
I think for members of parliament from areas of Canada who are not in the prairie or grain growing regions, this is one of the things we most strongly support. Many times in this parliament people might get the impression that the country revolves around eastern Canada, and members from western Canada are asked to support many money items which are large and mainly for the benefit of people in the east; but in terms of national unity I think one of the most important aspects of a united country is that we share strengths as well as weaknesses. In terms of the over-all importance of the grain industry to Canada, this is the type of expenditure which permits the support of all members from all parts of the country.

It should be $1 billion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
I would like to take issue, not with members of the official opposition but with whatever comes after that. Members of the NDP give much vocal muscle to whatever the problem of the moment is in this House, but if they were to read some of their own records, they would see much inconsistency.
I do not believe there can be much doubt that the business of railroading is extremely capital intensive. I believe that if someone was clairvoyant enough to predict three record crop years in succession, three successive record sales years, and a rail system built to move those crops within that short period of time, and then all that did not come about, the same people over there would be complaining about the tremendous growth in a transportation system which was not adequately used. They would be asking why so many rail cars had been purchased when there may or may not have been so much need.
I think anyone who has had experience in the past or responsibility for managing systems which are capital intensive must certainly understand that it is a judgment factor, and one of the things which has to be accomplished is to have a very high load factor or maximization of the use of capital. From the figures I have been able to read and from listening to speeches in the House, I feel that perhaps the railways and the government in concert have been able to predict fairly accurately. It may well be that the requirement to move the amount of grain which has been committed for export into eastern Canada will completely tax the system. In fact, it may not be able to deliver as quickly as one would hope. On the other hand, in terms of such tremendously capital-intensive industries as railroading perhaps investment decisions have not been all wrong and have come close to creating an optimum system.
I am quite interested in railroading. I have made it my business to learn a little about this industry. Hon. members who are contributing to this debate might be well advised to spend some time investigating the improvement in efficiency with which rolling stock is now used. I do not have any hard figures to illustrate the change in efficiency, but it has obviously improved very substantially. I suppose the introduction of computers and tracking systems by which railroads are able almost constantly to locate any rolling stock at any point in time has made a tremendous difference in terms of the effective use of the railway network. While railways are under severe criticism today by members of the New Democratic Party, I think the North American railways should at least be congratulated for operating one of the most effective networks I know.
It does not move enough wheat.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Members of the NDP very seldom if ever have the time or the interest to read business magazines. However, if they were to do that and if they were to read a number of American business magazines, they would find that one of the most often written about facts is the desperate state the U.S. railway system is in. As a matter of fact, in terms of investment in the state in which most of the U.S. railways have
June 5, 1978

maintained their stock, there is concern about being able not only to meet commitments in terms of moving grain, but also about the vast opportunities they have for developing coal mines and delivering that coal for export to Ontario and to other places. The industry is in serious jeopardy. When we talk about operating railways, given roadbeds and cars I do not think either Canadian Pacific or Canadian National need take a back seat to anybody. In terms of the size of the network these companies are operating, they should be congratulated on running a good railway.
I certainly do not stand here as any authority on how rates are established or on how demurrage is charged, but when the grain crop and the corn crop were being planted in eastern Canada this past spring, there was very serious concern about the availability of potash. For a period of time there were a number of fertilizer-blending plants which did not have the necessary potash available. I made inquiries about this. I was concerned about the number of railway cars which were available. In spite of the fact that there was a late spring, orders were not placed as soon as they normally were and deliveries were not accepted. I think this has a bad effect on the grain industry as well.
We cannot overlook the fact that one of the major reasons was the large number of cars which were in the United States. I noticed a number of reports in the press about the large number of cars still in the United States and about why the United States takes so long to turn cars around in their system and return them. I suppose it may well be that we have better cars in our system than they have in theirs, and they like to hang on to them and use them as much as they can; but in terms of this whole question it seems to me that that might be one of the areas which might be improved.
In conclusion, I would like to point out that in terms of the economy it seems to me that rebuilding the western railway network at this point in time is a very good decision. It seems to me that the many programs always being proposed by members of the NDP for making work and for providing more funding are no more important than this type of expenditure which is in the national interest. This type of expenditure would have a long-term effect. It would expedite the movement of one of our largest renewable resources. Surely it should have some precedence over some of the other proposals put forward by hon. members opposite.
I just wanted to make these few comments in this debate on the question of wheat, grain and grain movement. Grain movement to eastern Canada is a very important part of this. In terms of improvement over the past years, the great majority of the livestock and poultry feeders in eastern Canada will want to join me in congratulating the minister on the many forward steps he has taken.
Mr. Speaker, since the hon. member who has just spoken has not used up his full 20 minutes, I wonder if he would permit a question.

Certainly.

In view of the hon. member's comment that we cannot expect railroads to maintain all this equipment just to use in peak periods, I would like to ask him if he would then follow that through. Is he saying that bus companies, city transit companies and companies which move people on rails should maintain surplus equipment to take care of peak periods? Would he apply that also to people as he would to grain or any other products?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I come from an area which is very close to one of the largest cities in Canada, and I think it is just a plain fact that the same problem exists for moving people as for grain. There are a number of times in the peak requirement periods when a transit system does not have enough equipment to operate and they make the same judgment as the railways-the optimisation of their capital while providing the best level of service they can. I do not think either the railways or any of the other authorities moving people are able to invest economically in the kind of capital stock which would meet all needs at all times.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to take part in the debate on this opposition motion. It seems to me, after listening to the speakers who took part in the debate today, that to say that the grain situation in Canada is critical is an understatement. That is what we have heard from almost every speaker who has spoken in this debate, and they say it is because of the bottlenecks that have occurred at the Pacific ports, the other problems we encounter in trying to get the grain to those ports, and the fact that this will probably reduce Canada's opportunities not only to deliver the grain that is now sold but to compete in any new wheat sales that may come about.
The Canadian Wheat Board has confirmed that there will be a carryover of about 350 million bushels at the end of the current year. At present, most estimates show a 35 million bushel lag in the government's grain delivery schedule. According to the Palliser Wheat Growers' Association, the carryover is about 200 million bushels greater than the ideal minimum, which means that the grain economy will lose approximately $800 million in cash receipts which would accrue if the grain was delivered. Over the past few weeks we have seen reports and read in the newspapers that there have been up to 35 ships anchored in Vancouver harbour, some of these ships waiting up to five weeks to be loaded. According to one report, of these ships only two were at the loading berths. Of course, we have grain overflowing the elevators at most of the prairie points, and there is still a lot of grain in storage on the farms. Also, we have ships crowding in at both the western and eastern ports, but we cannot deliver the grain because of the lack of boxcars.
This boxcar problem is the result of an inadequate turnaround time, and also the result of difficulties in getting cars back promptly from the United States. This does not only

June 5, 1978
Grain
pertain to boxcars but also to hopper cars. Each ship that is laid over in the port costs the Wheat Board, the farmer, the consumer and the taxpayer demurrage costs amounting to some $5,000 a day. What we have is a minister who has not really taken any positive action to rectify the situation. He said in Winnipeg on May 11:
We may be getting close to what we can actually move out of the country during the course of a year.
In my estimation, that is not a very positive approach for the minister who is in charge of the Wheat Board to take. I should like to inform the minister and the federal government that there is more to Canada than the confederation-old transportation habits of moving goods inland east and west. There is also the north and the Hudson Bay Strait navigated by Hudson's Bay Company ships since 1668 and by grain ships through ports other than the port of Churchill since 1932.
The port of Churchill, as I have said in the House time and time again and as has been said by the Board of Grain Commissioners and the Wheat Board, is the most efficient grain handling port in Canada. Churchill's grain elevator operation has a turnover six times its storage capacity in less than the 100 days of the shipping season. That was the case in 1977. In the same year, the four dumpers allowed the elevator to unload slightly over 16,000 boxcars in 87 days of unloading. This gives an average of 184 cars per every eight hour working shift. This is what makes this port such an efficient grain handling operation. It handles no other commodity at present than grain and, believe me, it can handle grain without any problem. Thirty million bushels have been put through the port last year and 50 million bushels have been put through the elevator at a very small extra cost. I am glad to see the Chief Justice Emmett Hall has stated in his recommendations that the port should be upgraded to handle 55 million bushels a year. This would certainly take some of the pressure off the western ports.
Of course, the turnaround time on the boxcars is what must be considered. At present, the turnaround time out of Churchill is four days for a boxcar that goes up to Churchill, as compared to a five weeks waiting period for boxcars going to western or eastern ports. The travel distance from Yorkton, Saskatchewan is 722.5 miles. If you extend that to Moose Jaw, it is only a little over 100 miles more, which makes it only 822.5 miles as compared to the 1,301.7 miles to Vancouver from Yorkton or from Moose Jaw, give or take 75 to 100 miles. When you are shipping from Yorkton or Moose Jaw to Prince Rupert, it is 1,493.1 miles. The distance that has to be travelled to haul this grain to the west ports is twice that much, and when you consider the efficient turnaround time in Churchill, these cars could be back in service in one eighth of the time if more grain was moved out through Churchill instead of being hauled in these boxcars all the way out to the west coast.
I am not saying that the port of Churchill can compete with the western sea ports, but it would certainly relieve those sea ports if we only took the initiative to put on a double shift at the port of Churchill. CNR says it can handle more than 30 million bushels, and I want to compliment that company at

this time because in 1977 they had a well co-ordinated season and shipped 30 million bushels up to Churchill with no problem. It was in the elevator by October 1. However, no one really knows why the last two ships did not arrive in Churchill. This meant that three million bushels were left in storage in Churchill where we have a five million bushel storage capacity. It means money in the pockets of the port authorities when we have some grain stored there.
On May 2, 1978 the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) told the House of Commons that modernization of the outmoded prairie rail system and expansion of Pacific port facilities will increase grain exports by another 100 million bushels. The Federal government must take the initiative now to improve our economic position, ensuring that our raw resources reach export positions on time and help our balance of trade deficit. If the government would take action now and just give Churchill the opportunity, I am positive that 55 million bushels could be moved through the port.
Chief Justice Emmett Hall backs this up in his report, and the Churchill Development Board certainly substantiates those figures. Shipping through Churchill has increased by 7 per cent in the past year, and Lloyd's Underwriters of London have indicated that they would be more flexible in setting dates for the Churchill shipping season. Last year that extra 7 per cent was certainly a big benefit for us. At present, cargo and hull insurance is available only for ships which pass through the straits no earlier that July 23 and clear Churchill by October 20, with high risk insurance premiums charged after October 15. So we only have an 88-day shipping season.
The National Research Council has published a study indicating that the Churchill shipping season could be extended by 24 days on the average, an increase of 27 per cent in the season. The province of Manitoba royal commission inquiry into northern transportation indicated that the close of the season could be extended by 13 to 28 days. Can one imagine such an extension? That would provide the port of Churchill with another 10 million to 14 million bushels. With little capital investment and an extended season to November 10, more than 50 million bushels could be shipped annually through the port.
In conjunction with the Hudson Bay Route Association and the Port of Churchill Development Board, I urge the government to disregard the Bryden report and studies by the National Harbours Board condemning the future of the port of Churchill. Certainly that is what the Bryden report did. The minister found someone whom he knew would come up with a written report speaking out against the port of Churchill.
After the government spent $1.7 million on the Hall Report and $50 million to upgrade the town and port of Churchill, surely the Minister of Transport will not allow the findings of one or more reports to jeopardize the future of the port of Churchill. There has been a series of studies dating back as early as 1811 when Lord Selkirk settled the Red River Valley on the recommendation of his report on the Hudson Bay route by his peers in England. In the near future we may have oil
June 5, 1978

tanker traffic, uranium exports, increased grain shipment because of the world food crisis, sulphur from Alberta and potash from Saskatchewan.
Repeatedly I have asked the minister to consider shipping CIDA grain through Churchill. Those grains come under the direct control of the Canadian Wheat Board. When CIDA grain is being shipped through other ports, those ports are tied up, whereas Churchill could handle this additional grain. It could be scheduled not to interfere with the other grain shipping which goes through that port.
Must we wait for a second and third transportation foul-up before the minister takes action? In 1974 the government promised that the total grain handling system from the granary to the ship in the harbour would be revamped. Where is the long-term strategy? Why have western producers not been informed about it? Will the government tell the House why it is still unprepared to allow for greater provincial power-sharing in grain marketing?
The Hudson Bay Route Association unanimously passed a resolution this spring at its 35th annual meeting. The resolution cited increased operating costs of the St. Lawrence seaway, the political uncertainty of Quebec and the potential of the port of Churchill as being reasons for developing the northern port with provincial funds. It wants to see the three prairie governments taking a leading role in extending the shipping season out of the port of Churchill, expanding port traffic and enlarging port facilities.
If the federal government does not have the foresight to develop and utilize the port of Churchill to its full capacity, will the minister give that power to provincial governments? Will he turn that port over to provincial governments? Perhaps they can give the government $1 for that port. I am sure provincial governments would have that port working in no time. At this particular time, western premiers are prepared to take whatever action is necessary. If the minister would turn that port over, I am sure they would grab it.
The following resolutions were passed unanimously at the Hudson Bay Route Association annual convention: extension of the insurable shipping season out of Churchill; use of M. V. Arctic, a new semi-icebreaker bulk carrier, for grain shipments out of Churchill; construction of a new larger tug to assist ships when they arrive at Churchill; and the resumption of flour shipments through Churchill. The people in the Hudson Bay Route Association and the Port of Churchill Development Board are taking initiatives now to ensure the present and future success of Churchill. They have a commitment to the people of western Canada, the grain producers, the harbour people and overseas markets.
Where is the commitment of the federal government? Where is the commitment to fulfil the recommendations of the Hall report to meet the needs of people? We have been waiting a long time, and we are still waiting.

Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, in the last few minutes available I should like to bring into perspective some of the remarks which have been made today concerning this particular motion.
I want to highlight one glaring weakness in the positions of the government and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in respect of a very important part of the policy governing grain delivery in western Canada, that is, the Crowsnest pass rates. On a number of occasions the minister stated that he has maintained the Crowsnest pass rates. No one is taking issue with that. We are concerned about the minister's and the government's intentions for the future of the Crowsnest pass rates.
During the 1974 election campaign I ran for the first time. I was very attentive as to what the government said in respect of grain transportation and matters relating to agriculture. During the course of that campaign, the Winnipeg Free Press of June 11, 1974, reported the following:
Otto Lang said, "as long as the Liberal party forms the government and as long as producers wish to continue to deliver to the elevator of their choice, not one rail line will be abandoned.
Also, the Winnipeg Free Press of June 15, 1974 reported the following:
He (Trudeau) also reiterated his party's pledge to end any freight discrimination on the movement of meat, livestock and feed grains across Canada. This would not affect the Crowsnest special rates to aid the movement of grains for export to the west coast.
No sooner was parliament in session than the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board in an address to the Canada Grains Council in Edmonton said the following:
As part of the complete overhaul of the transportation system, we may have to examine the effect of the Crowsnest rates, particularly as they apply to domestic movements of grain.
Also he emphasized that the change was only a suggestion, and that the Crowsnest rates are a detriment to both rail carriers and producers.
In conclusion, the fact of the matter is that the minister has not given an unequivocal commitment to the Crowsnest pass rates in statutory form. In fact, Liberal candidates across western Canada are suggesting other methods of paying western Canadian farmers at the present time.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-PAYMENT OF LEGAL COSTS OF MEMBER OF FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 25 I asked the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) whether he would be prepared to pay the legal costs of a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who won a precedent-setting case. Perhaps I could have asked other ministers or members opposite if they were prepared to pay the legal costs of individuals who also won their cases against the government, such as Mr. Larry Stopforth and Mr. Walter Rudnicki.
I asked my question in the connotation as to whether the same consideration would be given to RCMP Corporal John Danch as was apparently being given to the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer). I raised this matter previously in correspondence and verbally with the present Solicitor General and his predecessor, but so far RCMP Corporal John Danch has not had his legal costs paid. His counsel, a distinguished Ottawa barrister, put the matter this way:
The simple fact of the matter is, that this man was dismissed, and in order to put the record straight and by reason of significant lapses on the part of the officials in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, it became necessary for him to appeal. His appeal was successful, resulting in his reinstatement which has the effect, apart from anything else, of setting the record straight. He has since gracefully retired. It seems to me, that it was never the intention of those who drafted this appeal procedure, that a successful appellant should swallow the substantial legal fees involved in putting the matter right.
The House would perhaps be interested in knowing a bit more about the way Corporal Danch has been "looked after", after twenty years on the force, after winning his case, and so on. After he resigned he was raided by about half a dozen members of the force and his house was searched and even socks and children's colouring books were taken pursuant to the search warrant, which stipulated only that they were looking for a tape recording, a copy of an RCMP report dated July 15, 1977 and a typewriter. Despite this, the members took away a host of memorabilia and personal items, in my opinion exceeding the jurisdiction of the warrant for search. They have since, I am informed, returned most if not all of what they took.
In addition, Corporal Danch, because of the delay in processing his appeal, had to draw unemployment insurance, and when reinstated he ran into administrative problems in the arrangements to repay. The force deducted a larger sum than agreed upon, and when Danch sought clarification weeks passed without any response, without any answers to his letters. I understand this has now been rectified.
My point is that John Danch has not been treated very well. He finally wrote a letter to a Halifax newspaper after I raised the matter in the House. It was a very reasonable letter and I should like to read part of it into the record. It states in part: When the recommendation for discharge was first made, I felt there were injustices implied and involved. I therefore pursued my rights through the proper channels, the courts, and did this not with the idea of personal material gain, but with a sense of obligation instilled in me through my many years of service.
From the events that have since transpired, whereby I have been harassed, and intimidated, I would have just cause for bitterness and animosity. This is not my

stature as I continue to have a high regard for the force. Even now with all the adverse publicity that is being generated against the force, my sympathies go forth to all the dedicated field personnel. It is indeed unfortunate that the force's problems and troubles can in large part be attributed to the treatment of its own personnel. It is in essence a strange attitude they possess whereby it is more important to justify matters than to correct procedures;-
Corporal Danch's letter in this Halifax newspaper has drawn comment and one 20-year veteran of the force responded. I am not going to mention his name for obvious reasons. He also had some interesting things to say about this matter. He said:
I read with great interest your letter to the editor in Saturday's Chronicle-Herald and for what it's worth, I say a very hearty "Bravo" to you.
He goes on to state in the letter:
You mention in your letter that we have no way of knowing whether unfair processing has really been stopped. I rather suspect that you inserted that for the benefit of the reading public. You can bet your life that it has not and will not until some drastic changes are effected in force policy.
I omit language which you might find unparliamentary, if not unfamiliar, Mr. Speaker. The letter continues:
Hats off to you. Keep up your fight. You won't get anywhere in the force (I'm assuming you're still a member) but you'll have the satisfaction of knowing you stood up for what you knew was right and that's a heck of a lot more than far too many of those-
I would censor the next word, Mr. Speaker, concluding the quotation as follows:
-management types can honestly tell their mirrors.
In conclusion, I want to suggest to the minister that the field personnel of the RCMP, the real backbone of the force, are apprehensive about what is happening. They know a double standard exists. They know, too, that there is not very much aid or comfort for them just because they follow orders. This is something that they were always taught-that if they followed orders they would be looked after. Now they are beginning to realize that unfortunately this is not always the case.
I would urge the minister to be equitable in cases such as this which can be symbolic and to bring in improvements in the way lower ranking personnel are treated. I ask once more, knowing this is the right and equitable thing, that the minister consider seriously exercising the discretion he has to pay the legal costs of an RCMP corporal who had no recourse but to resort to the courts regarding what he justly felt was a grievance, who won his case and is now faced with a legal bill for several thousand dollars and a very vindictive attitude expressed toward himself as a result of his success.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Young (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-PAYMENT OF LEGAL COSTS OF MEMBER OF FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Corporal J. Danch was discharged from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police by the commissioner under authority of RCMP regulation 173 on 15 December 1976. Subsequently, Corporal Danch made representation to the Federal Court of Appeal to review the matter of his dismissal. As a result of their review, the Federal Court, in a split decision, set aside the decision of the Commissioner due to a procedural error in the processing of Corporal Danch's recommendation for discharge. The court's decision then
June 5, 1978

meant Corporal Danch had been and continued to be a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and he was notified accordingly.
Following the federal court decision, Corporal Danch was again notified that his discharge was being recommended and he was given an extended period of time in which to submit an appeal. At the conclusion of the appeal period, Corporal Danch advised that it was his wish to voluntarily retire to pension.
Before resigning, Corporal Danch made application to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for reimbursement of his costs in presenting his case to the federal court of Canada. His request was reviewed and the legal opinion expressed was that the federal court dealt with the subject of party and party costs in rule 1408, which states:
No costs shall be payable by any party to an application to another unless the court in its discretion for special reason, so orders.
In the circumstances of this case, the federal court of appeal did not see fit to exercise its discretion in favour of Corporal Danch regarding costs.
The matter of solicitor and client costs was also considered. Corporal Danch is not entitled to costs from the Crown and there is no liability, therefore, whatsoever either in fact or in law.
The matter of an ex-gratia payment to Corporal Danch for his costs also received careful consideration but in view of the fact the commissioner's decision was not set aside on the merits of this case, but rather on a technical issue, neither the commissioner nor the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) are prepared to support a submission to Treasury Board. However, Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the hon. member that while the Solicitor General is not supporting the payment of his legal fees, Corporal Danch's file is being reviewed with respect to the question he has raised concerning the payment of unemployment insurance benefits.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: NATIONAL SECURITY-RIGHT OF MINISTERS TO KNOW HOW SECURITY PERSONNEL OPERATE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
NATIONAL SECURITY-RIGHT OF MINISTERS TO KNOW HOW SECURITY PERSONNEL OPERATE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Through you, Mr. Speaker, I wanted to bring to the attention of all hon. members that on December 14, 1977, at page 1856 of Hansard, I asked the then solicitor general, who has since left that post, whether he agreed with the novel theory the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that the solicitor general should not have any knowledge of whether or not the security forces of our country are acting legally or illegally, and whether or not he also agreed with the right hon. gentleman's novel theory that where security forces act secretly and illegally, the courts will protect us.
The solicitor general did not answer, apparently because the right hon. gentleman interrupted. I had occasion to ask the same question of the present Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) on February 6, 1978, as recorded at page 2571 of Hansard. I just want to put the position so that there is no doubt. The Prime Minister's reasoning is very strange indeed. He says that
Adjournment Debate
protection against illegal police activity lies with the courts. It is of benefit to look at exactly what the Prime Minister said:
We have the protection of the courts. If you want to break into somebody's house, you get a warrant. A court decides if you have reasonable and probable cause to do it. If you break in without a warrant, a citizen lays a charge and the police are found guilty. So this is control on the criminal side-
The trouble with this notion is that, first of all, the control by the courts which the Prime Minister refers to in the example he gives is only there if the police act lawfully and apply for a warrant. It is true that the application may be refused, not because there is illegality, but because the court decides there are insufficient grounds for granting a warrant. But the example used to support the Prime Minister's argument stops way short of meeting the real problem which is in issue, and that is the case where the warrant is refused and the police break in anyway, or when the police may well know there are insufficient grounds for obtaining a warrant and decide to break in, not just illegally, but secretly, without reference to a court.
Suppose I return from a weekend away from my residence and find there has been a break-in. Trusting the police, I call them to investigate. If they are the ones who committed the illegal break-in, does the Prime Minister really believe they will tell me about it and lay charges against themselves? The court will never even find out who broke in, let alone "protect us" from such illegal action.
Assume further that because I have practised law for years, I get suspicious and I go over the head of the police and ask the Solicitor General to investigate, which surely I have a right to do because he is the elected person ultimately responsible for police action. What is the Solicitor General going to say? Acting on the Trudeau theory, I will be told that the Solicitor General "should be kept in ignorance of the way in which the police are doing it". So how can I expect the Solicitor General to know, or even find out, because, again quoting the Prime Minister, "the government should keep its nose out of the operations of the police force".
It does not take a great deal of intelligence to realize that the courts can only act if someone lays a charge, or if the police lay a charge. Let us remember that the courts cannot convict unless someone proves the case with evidence. As is usually the case, the police investigate and produce the evidence. If the police are acting illegally and secretly, there is not much chance of an individual citizen ever finding the evidence. The court, or a judge, has no power to order charges or commence proceedings. In the absence of any responsibility to know or to act on the part of the Solicitor General, it is foolishness talk of the courts protecting the citizen from illegal activity of security forces or any other police force.
The Prime Minister went on to say that the government does not "have the authority" to act "in so far as the operations are concerned on the criminal side". This is bunkum. The Solicitor General, to whom security services report, certainly has the authority to act.

June 5, 1978
Adjournment Debate
The Prime Minister then remarked: "On the security side if you are fearful that this kind of thing is happening"-that is, illegal acts-"we have a royal commission of inquiry". Who orders the inquiry? Obviously, the government orders it. But can anyone believe that the only way the Solicitor General is to find out this is necessary is after some citizen, on his own, collects sufficient evidence, and, I suppose, makes it public, so that political considerations compel the government to act? The whole thesis of the Prime Minister has already been contradicted by former solicitor general Fox. It was because the then solicitor general finally decided to ask questions that caused him to act by setting up the present royal commission under Mr. Justice McDonald.
The entire argument of the Prime Minister is wrong. It is wrong because it contravenes the principle of ministerial responsibility which secures the rights of innocent people and is based on the premise that ultimately our elected representatives must ensure that those who report to them, and for whom they are responsible, exercise their functions within the law.
But it is also wrong because, when it comes to secret illegal activities of a police force, the courts cannot protect the citizen unless charges are laid, and it is highly unlikely that those who are breaking the law will investigate themselves and lay charges against themselves. The Prime Minister may not like our traditions of parliamentary democracy and responsibility under the rule of law, but he must not get away with changing them. I would like to know whether the present Solicitor General subscribes to the dangerous nonsense promulgated by the Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to respond to the question posed by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) on February 6, 1978 which is found at page 2571 of Hansard in which he refers to the theory of ministerial responsibility as advanced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at his press conference on December 9, 1977.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) agrees with the position as expressed by the Prime Minister during the course of his press conference. Surely the hon. member recognizes that in order to preserve the independence of the law enforcement agencies from political interference in their day to day operations, the politicians-and here I quote the Prime Minister- "who happen to form the government should be kept in ignorance of the day to day operations of the police force and even of the security force."
