-of the Prime Minister's press conference, he would have found that the Prime Minister stated on the security side that the principle has been that the police do not tell their political superiors about daily operations, but they do

have to act under the general directives and guidelines laid down by the government of the day. On the criminal side, members of the RCMP are accountable for their actions because of the necessity to present evidence in a court of law.
Theoretically, Mr. Speaker, an illegal act which remained secret could not be brought to the attention of any court. However, by the rigorous implementation of the RCMP commissioner's policy internally within the force and the safeguard, as proposed in the recently introduced act to amend the RCMP Act, of an independent third party review in the public domain as recommended by the Marin commission, illegal activities, if they occur, will certainly be brought to the attention of the courts.
In conclusion, it bears repeating that if the government finds any evidence of illegal activity, that evidence is turned over to the attorney general of the province in which the alleged illegal activity took place. This has been a long standing policy on the force and has been exemplified by the recent series of referrals to the provincial attorneys general as the result of the work of the commissions of inquiry.
The interest and concern of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) in this matter is certainly appreciated by the Solicitor General and I would like to thank the hon. gentleman for this opportunity to reply to his concerns this evening.

LABOUR CONDITIONS-YOUNG CANADA WORKS PROGRAM-FUNDS TO ASSIST STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since I first raised this question of Young Canada Works with the minister in this House on April 3, 1978, 1 have raised it on three different occasions. In correspondence and conversation with the minister's special assistant, Mr. Matt Graham, he has assured me that if there was to be a redistribution of funds, my constituency, along with Gander-Twillin-gate, would be first and second.
What bothers me is that we meet now on June 5, and having recently returned from my riding after interviewing a good number of university students who have been idle for over a month, and seeing the numbers who are graduating from grade 12 in the various high schools in my area, I see a crisis situation developing.
On March 2, I sent to the minister a special study that we had done on the grade 11 and 12 students in the high schools of Cape Breton-East Richmond which revealed that last summer 59 per cent of them were unemployed. A study that was done during the previous summer for the Department of the Secretary of State showed that in the Glace Bay area itself there was approximately 72 per cent student unemployment, and 44 per cent unemployment of non-student youth.
On April 25 I finally received an answer from the minister. He replied that he apologized for the delay, and I quote:
June 5, 1978

-because your letter and brief contained a great deal of material that needed to be examined in detail.
The major criticism offered by the minister of the results of the questionnaire was, and I quote:
It only contained high school students and not university students.... In comparing your 1977 allocation with the current one, you said that last year you received $424,000, while this year you received only $283,000.... I should point out that these figures are not entirely comparable as the former includes an additional amount that was granted through the reallocation of those funds that some constituencies were unable to use, whereas the latter does not.... Of course I am unable at this time, to determine the amount that will be available for redistribution this year but you may be sure that your constituency will be given every consideration when the redistribution exercise is undertaken later this spring.
It is now well beyong spring and we are into the summer season for college, technical and university students and will soon be into summer for high school students too. May I ask the minister, or his representative here this evening, to tell me truthfully whether a redistribution exercise is going to take place at all, or have the constituencies been allotted the total amounts they are going to get for Young Canada Works? There are a lot of very concerned students who are involved.
Just recently, a high school teacher in my riding from the town of New Waterford did a study in even more depth, using a better methodology than we used last fall, called the opinion analysis group technique. They found projected summer unemployment rates for high school graduates in the town of New Waterford of 71.6 per cent, and of these only 17.1 per cent would work long enough to be eligible for Unemployment Insurance Commission benefits. The percentage of students who see any possibility of getting jobs by moving out of the area was 11.3 per cent. Mr. Hollohan and his group went on to extrapolate from their sample and estimated there are over
14,500	unemployed people on Cape Breton Island and that 71.6 per cent of these are in the age group 16 to 24.
We recently witnessed the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) postponing what was expected to be an election in June or July because of what he termed the economic message for the government which was revealed by the polls. I think the government, in taking away the $2.5 million from the Young Canada Works program this year, has done a major injustice to the young people of this country and their parents, especially to those who have the misfortune to live in the low income and low employment areas. It is a sad thing to see a government so callous about what happens to its young high school graduates and to its college and university graduates that it will not make money available even on a short-term basis, knowing how difficult it will be for these people to find longer term employment. I wonder how many of the sons and daughters of MPs will be without employment this summer.
The government's policy is creating cynicism and alienation among many young people in this country. Many grade 12 students will have to cut out further education or demand increasing loans which will make the whole situation more expensive or self-defeating in any case. As a member of parliament from an area of heavy unemployment I can say it is
Adjournment Debate
a sickening experience to face this situation, and one can hardly exaggerate its effect in creating an increasingly negative attitude toward the country on the part of our young adults.
The figures which follow show the amount of money allocated through the Young Canada Works program in each of the three constituencies in Cape Breton for 1977 and 1978. For Cape Breton-East Richmond the amount was $283,000; for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso it was $289,000, and for Cape Breton-The Sydneys, $316,000. Those were the figures for 1978. I should have read the 1977 figures first. They were, for those three constituencies respectively, $424,000, $365,000 and $438,000. The number of registered student clients at Canada Manpower centres without employment was 3,505 in May, 1977, 3,986 in June, 3,613 in July and 3,513 in August when the largest number should have been working. This gives us a rough idea of what we can expect. In fact, the situation will be worse this summer.
And still we have a Prime Minister who talks about a just society with equal opportunity. To that, I say baloney-

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Milne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-YOUNG CANADA WORKS PROGRAM-FUNDS TO ASSIST STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in responding on behalf of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) I want to say that the concern expressed by the hon. member is most certainly shared by the minister and by others on this side of the House. The hon. member's interest in employment opportunities for youth is well documented as the result of his many interventions in this chamber on their behalf. I want to assure him that he is joined not only by the minister but, I am sure, by all members in the House.
Might I comment that the commission is making every effort possible to alleviate the student unemployment situation with the amount of funds which are available to it. Should additional funds become available the minister gives the undertaking that he will immediately inform members. The minister realizes that the Young Canada Works program has received a reduction in its level of funding over last year. However, it is not as extreme as the hon. member has stated. Under the 1977 Young Canada Works program $46 million was allocated to constituencies across the country and for the summer of 1978 the sum of $43.5 million has been allocated.
Young Canada Works is only one of the elements of the government's 1978 Canada summer youth employment program which has been funded at $96.2 million. Other elements include such other activities as the Canada Student Employment Centres, the job exploration program and the summer job core program which had its level of funding increased from $10 million to $12 million last year. As I mentioned in the House on April 3, 40 per cent of those who participate in the Canada Works programs are young people.

June 5, 1978
Adjournment Debate
As to the hon. member's question concerning the economic growth component, the minister forwarded a letter to all members of parliament on March 3, 1978 which explained this new initiative in detail. Some $50 million will be available to this program in 1978-79 for the funding of projects which will directly or indirectly result in the creation of continuing employment in the private sector. Available funds will be distributed on a provincial-territorial basis in approximately the same ratio as Canada Works funds are presently made available.
Projects are proposed by federal departments and agencies. In fact, the Treasury Board has approved some nine federal proposals involving approximately $27 million in economic growth component funds. Details as to the activities approved by the Treasury Board have been or will be announced by the ministers involved over the next few weeks. At that time the
initial impact of this program on the Atlantic constituencies will be available. Further proposals are still under review, and the minister hopes to be able to recommend the best of these to the Treasury Board as soon as possible.
In conclusion, I would like to add that, in addition to the initiatives we are considering under the economic growth component, the commission is looking at a variety of schemes through which Canada Works funds can be made available for activities of major economic benefit to regions. The minister points out that many of these discussions have centred around potential activities in the Atlantic provinces, particularly in the area of forest management.
